action_text:
Commissioner Adkinson stated she is the one who pulled this and she was hoping Peter Cranis, Tourism Development Office Director, could go over it with the Board.
Peter Cranis, Tourism Development Office Director, stated Marketing Support Program Grants are similar to what the County has had the last two years; they are cultural and support grants; this request is to approve the budget for $740,000 of which $120,000 is allocated to the five Commissioner Districts, so there is $20,000 for each District that the Commissioner can use for their purposes if each would like, but it is not a requirement; the last couple of years, four out of the five have done that; and then there is changes to the criteria, some strengthening of the wording in the criteria relative to what is allowable and also some clawback language now that is in there. He noted that is the gist of it, but he is happy to answer any questions.
Commissioner Adkinson asked if there were any applicants that were qualified who will not be receiving any funds.
Mr. Cranis pointed out this is for the next fiscal year; for this fiscal year all applicants who did qualify were going to receive funds except for one event that is not occurring on the sports side; therefore they obviously will not be receiving their funding; that is provided for in the criteria, that if an event does not happen for some reason then obviously there is no ability for the reimbursement.
Commissioner Adkinson inquired so there is no event that qualified that the $100,000 that Commissioners are getting to distribute, is being taken away from.
Mr. Cranis replied not that he is aware of.
Commissioner Adkinson stated her issue, and she brought it up last year because each Commission District is getting $20,000 to award to events that did not meet the minimum qualifications; last year she gave her District’s $20,000 back, and now the Commissioners have $25,000 to give to lifeguards, which is handy; her issue was partly because her understand is, the Tourist Development Commission (TDC) did not even discuss her concerns last year; and she asked if that is true that the TDC did not have an opportunity to discuss those.
Mr. Cranis replied they had gone through the full criteria; however, he does not believe there was any real discussion on that particular issue, but it was brought it.
Commissioner Adkinson inquired if the TDC last year found $100,000 to allow Commissioner’s to distribute, and they did again this year, does that mean it can do it every year and all of the sudden it becomes recurring funds, and the Commission could give that $100,000 per year to lifeguards; and she stated she knows that is a future question, but that is her issue with this.
Commissioner Feltner stated first of all it is not the Commissioners who appropriate the money; the Board of County Commissioners vote on it; the Board has only sought to get input from each of the Commissioners because historically over many years, there were Commissioners who said in their Districts certain things were not being supported and the Commissioner thought it was good; what he thinks could be done today to possibly satisfy things is to eliminate the entire $100,000 towards the small grants that do not meet those criteria for all the various things that were funded last year and put it all towards lifeguards; and he would make that motion today if Commissioner Adkinson would like that.
Commissioner Adkinson advised she would support that.
Commissioner Feltner asked if that is Commissioner Adkinson’s motion.
Commissioner Adkinson replied that is her motion.
Commissioner Feltner replied fine.
Chair Altman stated he wants to address a couple things that were brought up; the minimum criteria, these organizations in his mind were even more capable than some of the items that were funded; these were wonderful programs that provided a lot of resources to the communities and many of them were significantly financially strapped; he thinks they were good programs; the minimum criteria was somewhat of a loophole because it is a broad-based set of criteria and some of them may apply and some not; and he does not think it was a misuse of public funds. He went on to say secondly, he thinks it is very helpful that the people that are elected and that the public votes for that are vetted more than any other group has a voice; they know what the need is in their local communities; by the way this money did not go just to local communities because he recommended a program that was not even in his District, but it was so important and so critical, it was so strapped that he felt it appropriate; he did not just look at the District; he wanted to point out that the Commissioners having their own involvement was very healthy and very good; and he thinks that going to lifeguards is not bad, although it is not going to solve the lifeguard problem, and there are other funding sources that must be looked at beyond the TDC. He noted he does not think anyone can expect the TDC to fully fund that; he thinks the Board should have a broad-based level of participation and it should be specifically related on how it provides the services and who benefits; he thinks everyone should have a little skin in the game; it does not solve the problem that this Board is going to need to solve; and this appropriation as small as it was, did solve some significant problems for some of the smaller organizations.
Commissioner Feltner stated the $25,000 he asked for in the last TDC meeting, that was unplanned but they were in that moment trying to do a raise for the lifeguards because they are competing with area pools; the $25,000 that the TDC appropriated for that, that was on the Agenda today, was taken from the Capital Fund; that was done because they TDC agreed as a Council that it was not going to spend money on capital this year because it had less than a million dollars, somewhere in the $900,000 range; the TDC wanted to wait until that was replenished; and it was from those funds that the TDC took the $25,000 from to help shore up the lifeguards. Commissioner Feltner asked Mr. Cranis if that sounds correct.
Mr. Cranis responded affirmatively; he stated he was going to ask for clarification on this $100,000; and it does come from the cultural budget, so if that is the budget where the Commission wants to move dollars to lifeguards, it would be great if it was part of the motion.
Commissioner Feltner stated he will amend the motion to take the $100,000 from the cultural fund to fund lifeguards.
Commissioner Adkinson stated she will second that.
Chair Altman asked if the Board is able to do that, if those funds are specifically designated for that area, and does the Board have the legal ability to do that, as he knows it was a formula that was passed by the public and provided for in the Statutes.
Morris Richardson, County Attorney, stated under State law the Board can; and he will have to take a look at the local budget Ordinance to see if it has to be amended or adjusted.
Mr. Cranis noted that is part of the budget where it reads up to, and those funds could be moved to marketing and from there be directed to lifeguards.
Attorney Richardson advised they just will not go directly from cultural, they will pass through to another fund.
Chair Altman commented it will be looked at if there is a problem, and the Board can address that; and he asked if there is any other debate on the motion.
The Board approved the original allocation of $100,000 for funding District Commission office event grants be shifted from the cultural fund to fund the lifeguards.
body: Brevard County Board of County Commissioners
title: Approval, Re: Tourist Development Council FY 2026-2027 Marketing Support Program Funding, Criteria, Application and Event Income/Event Expense Worksheet

action_text:
Rick Heffelfinger stated whenever the County plays around with pay raises that is not a one-time event; the County has thrown some money at a pay raise from the tourist capital facilities fund; and his question is what happens after 2025/2026; he commented those guys have gotten a pay raise so that is going to be a reoccurring cost; and he was wondering what that would do to the cost of that funding effort in the future, because people know it is going up by $25,000 to help pay those guys; he is not sure how many employees that is and how much the raise is; but that $25,000 is going to be reoccurring every year after that with the lifeguards. He mentioned he was wondering if anybody has done that math.
Commissioner Feltner stated he will attempt to answer that on behalf of the Tourist Development Council (TDC); Fire Rescue has already decided to give the lifeguards a raise as a means for the County to stay competitive because it is competing with area pools to hire the lifeguards for the summer; what he did at the TDC was to ask for the $25,000 to help shore that up for the summer; but going forward he does not envision a time when the County will be paying lifeguards less; and that is something Fire Rescue will build in the budget in the future. He went on to say he would imagine tourism tax will continue to contribute towards the lifeguard cost.
Mr. Heffelfinger stated and that should go up, yes.
Chair Altman asked if Mr. Heffelfinger is upset that the County gave its lifeguards a raise.
Mr. Heffelfinger replied no, he does not have the history of it; he does not know what they are currently making; he does not know how much they received; he asked if the $25,000 goes towards that salary; and if that is a reserve that they could get a bump like that.
Chair Altman explained what was done so people know, there have been some serious deaths on the beaches and they are understaffed tremendously; he also pulled this Items because he wanted to thank staff for the incredible work they have done; they were able to look at reserve funds and provide for an increase in pay; it has really enabled the Board to fill a serious backlog; and it is going to save lives. He continued by saying it is good that the Board did this; to answer Mr. Heffelfinger’s questions, the answer is yes, these pay raises will not go away; and he asked what the scale was.
Jim Liesenfelt, County Manager, advised the lifeguards are paid about $16 an hour and it went up to $20-$21 per hour.
Chair Altman commented and there has been tremendous response.
Mr. Liesenfelt responded affirmatively stating he is getting a thumbs up from those in the back of the room that they are receiving a positive response in recruiting.
Chair Altman noted it is tough to fill those positions, it is a very difficult job; he was reading the requirements to be a lifeguard; this is serious and many are Emergency Medical Technicians (EMTs); he thinks it is good and hopes the County continues to pay its lifeguards an affordable wage to get the best and brightest because beach safety is so important; he would like to thank Commissioner Feltner for what he did in the TDC; the County has some real challenges out there; there is probably a lot more that needs to be done; he thinks everybody needs to be pulling in the same direction; and there is a need for diverse and broad funding because Brevard County has more beach than any other county in the State. He mentioned the economic impact of tourist dollars, if the County starts seeing a lot of deaths, he thinks one year there were nine; fortunately the lifeguards have been really incredible in preventing deaths; this will help them; and he is excited about this, and wanted to commend staff.
Mr. Heffelfinger added he went to the Mayor’s breakfast and enjoyed Sheriff Ivey’s speech; there were a couple comments made taking shots at this dais about not funding certain beaches; he does not know where the County is on that; and he asked if there in any anticipation for TDC funding on some of those beaches that cried about not having enough cities, because he is not exactly sure where or which beaches that currently have lifeguards in Brevard County, through the TDC.
Chair Altman commented that he thinks the Board is going to have a lot of discussions about that; he cannot predict what will happen; and as the Board goes through the budget process, he is hopeful the Board can continue to look at making the beaches safer.
Mr. Heffelfinger responded by saying okay.
Chair Altman continued by saying it is amazing that staff and lifeguards have done as good a job as they have with the resources that they have been given; and he is hopeful that the Board will continue to give them more.
Mr. Heffelfinger inquired if all those lifeguards are the Fire Rescue type or if the County takes college kids and part-time them.
Commissioner Feltner advised by saying the County relies pretty heavily on high school students when they are out of school to cover the summers; and in fact the County celebrated two 16-year old students at the Fire Rescue awards just a few weeks ago.
Mr. Heffelfinger stated so they go through a course offered by Fire Rescue to certify them for that.
Commissioner Feltner replied he is getting nods from the back, so yes.
body: Brevard County Board of County Commissioners
title: Approval, Re: FY 2025-2026 Incremental Funding for Lifeguard Pay Raises

action_text:
Jacque McPhillips stated for many years she has been an affordable housing developer; currently, for the last several years, she represents non-profit organizations that are developing affordable, both rental housing and subdivisions, the first time homeownership; what she passed out and the Board is probably aware of it, there are news laws coming down the pike that are Florida legislature; one was House Bill (HB) 399, the other Senate Bill (SB) 594, one of which really has to do with changes and every local governments Local Housing Assistance Plans (LHAP) as far as allowing factory-built homes being allowed as January 1, 2027, and other extended areas, residential developments; and the other law primarily deals with State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) funds. She mentioned currently Florida housing had a 20 percent cap on the amount that any local government could give of their SHIP on manufactured homes; it is repealing that so local government could give any amount that they want; they are seeing a lot of things coming down the pike, having now to do with factory made housing for affordable housing because of the sheer cost of land escalating, along with construction costs escalating; it is getting more difficult to develop true affordable housing with income limits and so forth; and she thinks the State government is trying the best it can, to come up with some new provisions that will open up or help create more affordable housing, both for rental and especially for first time homeownership. She continued by saying on June 23 the coalition will be hosting a webinar that she thinks all local governments, counties as well as cities, will be listening into because it is going to be basically a tutorial explaining the law, how it affects local government, and how it affects the citizens; she is sure the Department of Housing and Human Services will be on that call as well; one of the Items which has to do with SHIP is why she is there today, as she understands it, after discussions with Nicole Tenpenny, Executive Director of Community Housing Initiatives, Inc. (CHI), works with all eligible applicants for SHIP on qualifying them and so forth; they are serving about half of what they used to just because of the higher cost; she is very much in favor of this; and the request is to please reconsider allowing SHIP dollars to be used on manufactured homes, no differently than on site-built homes, that will allow many more families to be served with SHIP.
Chair Altman commented he is sure this is something the Board will look at in the future.
Ms. McPhillips stated one last thing, she has been invited to go to one of two factories built here in Florida, manufactured by executives of the Florida manufactured home, the Florida Housing Coalition introduce her to them; they have offered graciously to do a private tour; and she will be bringing not-for-profit organizations herself and reach out to County staff to see some of them would maybe like to become more educated on today’s manufactured homes and if any of the Commissioners would like to attend.
Chair Altman stated it is his understanding that she is not just talking about mobile homes; some of these manufacture homes look like beautiful homes.
Ms. McPhillips stated mobile homes, as she has been trying to get educated now more on the whole subject, actually stopped being built in 1976, 50 years ago; they were more mobile and kept the wheels on.
Dr. Lance Armstrong stated he is accompanied by Amanda Kind and they are representing Rolling Thunder Chapter 1; it is the largest Chapter in Florida and the third largest in the nation or a nationwide organization that is simply an advocacy group; they are not a motorcycle club, they are searching for their missing troops like his cousin, a pilot who took off in World War II; Rolling Thunder has done a lot to help the US Department of Defense (DOD) restructure under one roof in Hickam where many of the remains found are brought for proper identification, preparation for burial, and return to family soil; and the organization in this area has led the nation in posting that Prisoner of War (POW) flag under the American flag in all 84 schools. He continued by saying they are posting the statement that they want their missing returned; there are almost 80,000-plus since World War I; of that number it is believed that approximately 27,000 can be found; annually the would go to Washington D.C. for 32 years; in 2019, when 1.7 million motorcycles showed up, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) organized a little statement to them saying, “Don’t do this again, please make it State run”; they have played by that rule for five years and he has been asked to run it two of the five years, 2021 and 2023; it has also been in Daytona, Port Charlotte, and Punta Gorda; he messed it up so bad they have blocked it here for the next five years; and he will be coming back to the Board year-after-year. He went on to say this is their big first year and he wants to thank the County and the Board for allowing them to use the brand new $8.2 million amphitheater for one of the three major events they have going on this weekend; like in Washington on Friday night, Gold Star family members would carry a beautiful flame of freedom in front of the Vietnam Wall; about 30,000 of them would go there, not one speaking; they have upped the quality of that night by having Texas Roadhouse complimentarily feeding the Gold Star family a dinner; these folks will come together, meet, break bread, and heal; then his group will ride in from Fish Lips and the Sandbar where they are doing their ride registration, and escort them after dark, about 8:30 p.m., on that walk; and if there are patriotic people in Brevard County that wish to support their Gold Star family, please consider being at the Brevard Veterans Memorial Center on Friday night at about 8:00 p.m. He noted Saturday is the festival where they have some great music, vendors, and they hope the public comes and enjoys the music at the Veterans Memorial Center; Sunday is the ride for freedom; they are riding down State Road 3 from the Veterans Memorial Center just like last week’s law ride; they will turn left and go across Pineda Causeway to A1A and up through Cocoa Beach; Cocoa Beach Police Department (PD) will escort them; every sheriff in every location has supported this, but Sheriff Ivey says he cannot; he will help them get on State Road 3 with a couple of deputies, but he wants the folks who reside on State Road 3, south of 520 to know that they are coming down that route on Sunday at about 11:00, leaving the Veterans Memorial Center; and he asked people to please consider coming out front, waving American flags and supporting this organization in that manner. He commented as they come up through Cocoa Beach, he hopes the same will occur again as it had in those two years; the organization hopes that the public knows that this is a center for the State of Florida and this is a Florida event, but they are not playing by that rule this year; that is the Texas emblem and they are talking to Mississippi, both North and South Carolina chapters are considering, and Georgia is coming; this might be turning into the southeast United States Memorial Day Weekend rolling Thunder Ride for Freedom Event; and he hopes the County is aware of that for the next four or five years. He thanked the Board for its support; he stated if he may ask, they are considering the fifth, it is about a 20-foot wide median on Sykes Creek, and they would like a little sign there that is lit saying Rolling Thunder Event in this direction; and they hope that is allowed.
Chair Altman stated by the way for those listening a Gold Star family is a family who has lost a loved one in the service of this country and who have paid the ultimate sacrifice; he certainly appreciates them; and the County cannot do enough for them.
Commissioner Feltner asked if they have the sign and are asking if they can place the sign out there.
Dr. Armstrong replied it is waiting to be rented; it is just a little trailer sign that says event this way, they cannot borrow them from the County.
Jim Liesenfelt, County Manager, inquired if it is an electronic message board sign.
Dr. Armstrong advised it is just a lit sign that says 'Rolling Thunder this way.'
Commissioner Feltner asked if a motion would be appropriate to allow them temporarily to do that.
Mr. Liesenfelt replied he has no idea what the sign ordinance might be, so yeah.
Commissioner Feltner asked if an exemption from the sign ordinance for this event.
Dr. Armstrong replied he will guarantee the sign will not block any sort of public view, roadway, or anything like that; and he commented still today when he mentions Brevard Veterans Memorial Center to many of his patients, they ask where that is.
Tad Calkins, Assistant County Manager, stated it sounds like the sign is going to be placed in the right-of-way so if Dr. Armstrong wants to work with Public Works they can get him the appropriate permits to have that happen.
Dr. Armstrong commented it is back from the intersection on the median.
Chair Altman asked if a motion is needed.
Commissioner Feltner inquired if there needs to be a motion to allow them to do that for this event.
Mr. Liesenfelt replied affirmatively.
Commissioner Feltner stated he would make that motion.
Mr. Liesenfelt interjected by saying and to waive the fees if necessary.
Commissioner Feltner added and to waive any necessary fees, to have the sign temporarily for the event.
The Board approved waiving any necessary fees and exemption of the sign Ordinance, to allow Rolling Thunder, Inc. to place a temporary illuminated traffic sign in the right-of-way at Sykes Creek Parkway for the Rolling Thunder Event taking place at the Brevard Veterans Memorial Park Amphitheater on May 22 – 24, 2026.

action_text:
Chair Altman called for a public hearing to consider an ordinance placing a referendum on the November 3, 2026, ballot to renew the one-half cent infrastructure sales tax for the SOIRL Program.
Virginia Barker, Natural Resources Management Director, stated this Item is asking the Board to consider placing before the voters a referendum to renew the existing one-half cent infrastructure sales tax that funds the SOIRL Program; in 2016, Brevard County residents chose to invest in restoring the Indian River Lagoon (IRL) following a series of harmful algal blooms, fish kills, and significant seagrass loss; the voter approves sales tax created a dedicated trust fund that allows the County and its municipal, private, and non-governmental partners to implement projects that reduce nutrient pollution, remove legacy muck, upgrade wastewater and septic systems, and restore natural ecological filtration systems; over the past decade, the program has completed more than 130 projects, leveraged over $127 million in State and Federal grants, and helped thousands of homeowners and businesses reduce nutrient pollution on their private property; during this time, excess nutrient levels have declined, harmful algal blooms and fish kills have lessened, and seagrass and fisheries recovery has begun; and while this progress is encouraging, continued pollution reduction is necessary to meet water quality targets, and restore Lagoon health. She continued to say the current sales tax expires December 31, 2026, renewal, if approved by the voters, is estimated to generate approximately $800 million, over 10 years for continued Lagoon restoration efforts; the actions before the Board today would approve the ordinance, placing renewal referendum on the November 3, 2026, ballot, extending the existing Interlocal Agreement with the municipalities, contingent upon voter approval, and approve the ballot language for transmission to the Supervisor of Elections; approval of these items does not renew the tax, it will provide Brevard County voters the opportunity to decide whether they wish to continue this locally dedicated investment in restoring and protecting the IRL; and staff is requesting the Board’s consideration of those three recommended actions, and she is happy to answer any questions.
Mitchell Roffer stated he received his doctorate in biological oceanography from the Rosenstiel School, Miami; he has since served 20 years on the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) biodiversity science team; he is presently on the Science, Technology, Engineering, and Modeling (STEM) Advisory Committee, as part of the IRL Council; to save the SOIRL Program plan prioritizes and delivers projects that reduces pollution, removes legacy nutrient loads, and to restore natural filtration systems while tracking progress and effectiveness over time; what is important about this plan, in addition to looking at the science, is it provides transparency, and transparency through project citizens oversight, public meetings, and educational tools are provided for the residents to understand what is going on; it does not take much for someone to know what is happening with the Lagoon, particularly with this Program to just go on the website; and he is trying to stay away from some of the false information on Facebook, and go to the website itself, which shows what is going on. He mentioned depending on whom a person talks to, it has taken 30 to 50 years to get to this point in the Lagoon, and it is certainly going to take at least that much time to get the Lagoon back to the point of where it can help itself; there is nothing that can be done other than stop the pollution to get it back to its natural cycle, which he hopes to do as a scientist; it is important to know that the IRL provides a strong economic boost to the County, as well as the health of the County depending on it, and not just the health of the animals associated with the Lagoon; but the people around the Lagoon who are influenced by algal blooms, as well as eating the fish that may be toxic themselves. He advised he is here today to hope the Board would fully support putting this one-half cent tax back on the referendum for the taxpayers; hopefully, good management will continue with Ms. Barker and her staff for what they have been doing for the last 10 years; and it seems 10 years has gone by fast and are just barely toughing the problem.
Jim Moir stated he is with the Marine Resources Council (MRC) and he is also the Indian Riverkeeper; he lives in Martin county and he was engaged in the early days of the SOIRL Program and he applauds that Commission and this Commission for continuing to keep the SOIRL Program going; the seven other counties that live up and down the IRL look up to this Commission and what it has done, it truly sets a high standard for how a community cares about the IRL, and is willing to do something about it; he is hopeful that the Commission persists and continues, because progress is beginning to be seen that this Program actually has worked, and has reduced some of the negative inputs that the decades of misuse have allowed the IRL to become what it has; and he expressed his thanks for considering the resolution and he hopes the Board moves forward with it, and that it actually exceed the goal of $800 million. He added, that is an amazing amount of money that the Board could actually leverage to get something positive done for something that all care so much about.
Phil Stasik expressed his thanks to the Board for its service to the community; he stated it is amazing that 10 years ago, he and many of his friends that are here today stood before the Commission and asked it for its support of this wonderful program, that works; he expressed his thanks to Ms. Barker and her team for making this reality; the IRL estuary is the beating heart of Brevard County; it is known that it has been in trouble for probably 80 years when the decline began, as people moved in the community they began impacting the community in negative ways; and it has literally only been in the last 10 years that they as a group, thanks to the courage and the leadership, the wisdom of the previous Commission 10 years ago, that they were able to begin reviving the beating heart of the community. He went on to say now it is 10 years later they all got up and looked in the mirror, and said, “Oh my gosh, has 10 years gone by.”; they sure have and here they are again, but now it is up to the Board because they are all looking at it to have the courage, wisdom, and leadership to bring the SOIRL back to the people, and to vote again in November for the one-half sales tax; the cost is minuscule; the benefits are awesome; he can speak about this personally, because over the years, he has been an oyster gardener, worked on Spoil Islands, done cleanups on the shore, spent hours diving on the bottom of the Lagoon to clean it up; he saw it with his own two eyes and he felt it with his own two hands; the SOIRL Program works; and measuring the restoration of the seagrasses and seeing the fish returning, it is going to take a lot more than just this amount of money that had been done over the past 10 years, and it is going to take another 10 years and maybe another 10 years after that; but the one-half cent sales tax is a simple solution to a complex problem. He reiterated 10 years later, they are standing here asking the Board again to please say yes to bring the SOIRL Program back to the voters so that they can say yes.
Gordon Nelson provided the Board with a handout; he stated he is located in The Hamlet near the southeast corner of Lake Washington Road and Turtle Mound Road; Turtle Mound Road is the west watershed boundary line, and he is three miles from the Lagoon; there are 59,438 septic tanks within the watershed of Brevard County; SOIRL estimates the nitrogen from his properties and the 50 properties in The Hamlet are 1.6 pounds per year, 12 properties are 3.1 pounds per year, 18 properties are under 10 pounds per year, and eight properties are 31 pounds; that yields 210 pounds per year for 42 homes, plus 248 pounds per year for the eight properties along the Eau Gallie River ditch; the cost to upgrade 50 properties is $1.1 million, at $22,000, which is in fact, not going to be enough; clearly spending over $1.1 million is a waste of money; the current process of giving grants of $20,000 to high emitters, but only $6,000 at the low end is blatantly unfair; in fact, 42 low emitters properties should not be required to replace their systems, with all of the environmental damage involved; and the average emitter is 29 pounds per year, 65 percent of that is 18.9 pounds per year, 42 properties are already lower than that achieved by the emitter after upgrade. He added, if a person looks at NSF 245, which is the test for septic systems for systems with low nitrogen influent, nitrogen is actually added to the test; to assess whether the septic systems gets 65 percent and is actually adding nitrogen; it is not established, therefore, that low influent systems achieve any reduction; replacing 60,000 septic tanks at $20,000 is $1.2 billion; the current State legislated date of July 2030 would clearly not be met by far; the plan for next decade has $233 million to improve sewerage treatment, convert septic-to-sewer, and septic upgrades, that is far from $1 billion to $1.5 billion that is going to be needed; Vero Beach has a hybrid system for 1,500 homes; its Septic Tank Effluent Pumping (STEP) system has half of the costs with minimal installation and environmental damage; and Brevard needs better technology. He stated the renewal and the sales tax is not ready for prime time, given the sales that the septic tank issues has that he mentioned; a rational comprehensive plan needs to be in place and it is not yet there, or homeowners may well vote no.
Captain Blair Wiggins stated he is the host of Blair Wiggins Outdoors, he is a lifelong resident of Cocoa Beach, and he is the founder of the Indian River Clam Restoration Project; he just wanted to say that his fans and he are in support of keeping the one-half cent sales tax on the ballot; the programs that SOIRL is funding now, he would hate to see those go away; and he reiterated they are definitely in support of keeping the sales tax on the ballot.
Vince Lamb stated he is speaking today on behalf of the Brevard IRL Coalition; he is sure that the Board could remember back in March when they requested assistance from the Trust for Public Land (TPL) to come forward and perhaps help them with some of the elements of campaigning for this; he wanted to share with the Board that the TPL conducted a public opinion survey of likely 2026 November ballot for Brevard County voters and believes, based on the results that the renewal of the SOIRL one-half cent sales tax has a good chance of passing; therefore, the IRL Coalition recommends that the Brevard County Commission place the measure on the November 3 ballot; most people recognize the efforts of the past nine years of the SOIRL Program having resulted in seagrass recovery of more than 10,000 acres; and many people believe that the Brevard County portion of the IRL remains in poor to fair condition, substantially improved from 10 years ago, but not yet back to anything resembling good condition. He stated the Brevard IRL Coalition is prepared to launch a campaign to inform voters about this referendum and why they should vote for it, as done in 2016; volunteers are currently being recruited to get ready for an active campaign in September and October; the Board’s consideration is greatly appreciated with this matter today; and the Brevard IRL Coalition looks forward to getting to work on it.
Gary Aguinaga stated he is a longtime resident of Brevard County since the 60’s and he presently lives on the IRL in Cocoa; he is a marine engineer by degree and has volunteered many hours a year with all of the many programs that all of those great organizations and scientists, engineers, and other folks do to help with trying to turn this Lagoon around; he is here today because he cares deeply about this Lagoon, he grew up here when it was pristine, and he would love to preserve that for his children and their children; he also cares deeply about this County and he thinks it is clear about what somebody said that this Lagoon is the heartbeat of the County, but the direct tie to the long-term well-being viability and the economic viability of this County is critical to having a healthy Lagoon, in terms of property value, inward growth, development, business success, and tourism; and it does not work with a dead Lagoon. He continued to say he is present to ask the Board to consider, not only approving this to be on the ballot, but to do it unanimously; as the Board goes about its circles of influence to help raise awareness of just how critical this issue is to the County, he thinks it is critically important at this point, after 10 years, that as others have said, there is visible evidence now; there is scientific evidence and visible evidence that it is beginning to work; but to stop funding now would present such a huge challenge as it has just begun, and he thinks would be devastating, not only financially, but to the hundreds and thousands of volunteers who got behind this team effort to try to turn this Lagoon around. He mentioned the root causes have not been solved yet, there is a lot of reactive fixes between the filter feeders like clams and oysters, and seagrass growing, et cetera; there are still too many septic systems, still have a huge stormwater runoff problem, still have municipalities that have been a bit slow to require low-impact development with developers, et cetera, and the more concrete and asphalt put down, the more stormwater runoff and nutrients will go into the Lagoon in the future; and he thinks now is the time to double down, continue what was started, and do the right thing.
Matthew Nylen stated he is from the Brevard Democratic Environmental Caucus and he expressed his thanks to the Commission for the public and transparent process that has brought it to this critical point of decision on the renewal of the SOIRL Program; he is confident today for a positive outcome from the Board; and he looks forward to the opportunity to build a broad coalition of Brevard County residents, who value the quality of life in the County, and share that the IRL is the crown jewel that anchors the area's environment.
Anne Conroy stated on behalf of the Space Coast Chamber of Commerce, it supports allowing the citizens of Brevard County the opportunity to vote on the renewal of SOIRL for an additional 10 years; meaningful outcomes from SOIRL is already being seen through critical infrastructure improvements, water quality projects, septic-to-sewer conversions, and restoration efforts taking place throughout the County that are all backed by data and transparency; continuing this momentum is important, not only for the environment, but for the long-term economic health and resiliency of the region; the health of the IRL is directly tied to the communities quality of life, environmental sustainability, tourism industry, property values, and long-term economic vitality; a healthy Lagoon supports local businesses, attracts visitors and talent, help retain that talent, protect one of the region’s most valuable and natural economic assets; and with the economic and population growth Brevard is forecasted so see in the next 10 years with the accompanying environmental stresses, it is more important than ever that this essential work continues. She added, the Chamber believes that the residents of Brevard County should have the opportunity to decide on the future of the Lagoon.
Elizabeth Neville, Director of Environmental Law and Policy for the Save the Manatee Club, stated Save the Manatee Club is a nonprofit dedicated to protecting manatees and their habitat; the Club strongly supports placing the SOIRL referendum on the ballot to allow the Brevard County voters the opportunity to continue investing in the long-term health of the IRL; since its creation, SOIRL has funded critical restoration and water quality improvement projects throughout the Lagoon watershed; these investments have supported septic-to-sewer conversions, muck removal, stormwater improvements, wastewater infrastructure upgrades, and habitat restoration projects aimed at reducing nutrient pollution entering the Lagoon; together, these projects are helping improve water quality and ecosystem health across the region; these efforts are especially important for Manatees; over the last decade the IRL has experienced catastrophic seagrass loss, largely driven by nutrient pollution and harmful algal blooms; seagrass is a primary food source for Manatees and its decline has had devastating consequences on the East Coast Manatee population; and between December 2020 and April 2022, Florida experienced the deadliest unusual mortality ever on record, during which 1,255 manatees died, primarily from starvation linked to the severe seagrass loss in the Lagoon. She stated the IRL program provides funding for projects that improve water quality and restores submerged aquatic vegetation directly supporting the recovery and long-term survival of the State’s marine mammal; environment and economics deeply entwine when it comes to the benefits of Lagoon restoration; the Lagoon generates approximately $28.3 billion in economic value and attracts millions of visitors annually, meaning water quality decline can carry serious economic consequences for the surrounding communities; and poor water quality and harmful algal blooms contributed to average property value losses of approximately $36,000 per home, and roughly $2.7 billion in total housing market losses in just eight year during the crisis. She concluded by saying in summary, Save the Manatee Club strongly supports placing the SOIRL renewal referendum on the ballot; SOIRL is making a measurable difference, but the work is far from complete; and with State and Federal funding in flux, the County cannot afford to lose local investments, for the sake of the Manatees, the environment, the economy, and the communities continued commitment to the IRL remains essential.
Lisa Ruckman expressed her thanks to the Board for everything it does for the County; she stated she appreciates the staff because every time she has called with a question, they have always been helpful, and making sure her questions get answered; she is a volunteer with the Lagoon Coalition and the East Merritt Island Community Association (EMICA), which is basically the east zip code for Merritt Island; EMICA has seen improvement with the Lagoon and it is happy to see the progress that has been happening, but it is still looking forward to having the water be clearer, to having the dolphins be a little healthier because she knows that they are struggling a bit, to be able to see the fish in the water, and to have healthy fish to be able to fish again; there are a lot of homes that are near the water on Merritt Island and many of those still have the septic tanks that are probably too close proximity to the Lagoon; EMICA is grateful for the projects that have been happening, that are still going to be happening in the area, and for the financial assistance because it can be a big deal for people who are replacing septic tanks to a better septic tank, or for the ones who are able to connect to the new sewer conversion; and they would like for the tax dollars of the SOIRL Program to work hard, focusing and finding those things which are going to make the most impact, and trying to use finances strategically. She added, the people are worried about their property values and with improving the Lagoon, property values increase, and if things are not handled well and there are more algae blooms, that that will not assist with property values; the people would like this to continue seeing success in all the education that has been done with the Program, the cleanup and all of the restoration efforts; and in fact, there is a project starting in her neighborhood and there will be a meeting on Tuesday that staff will talk about.
Laurilee Thompson provided the Board with a handout of St. Johns River Water Management District (SJRWMD) 2025 seagrass update; she stated she lives in Mims, a long time river rat, she brought the Board proof, absolute proof, and the timing is wonderful for the SJRWMD to do a press release a couple of days ago, showing that the seagrass is absolutely increasing in the IRL; this press release is based on the 2025 update, which is done every two years, and the next one will come in 2027; it was shown that in 2023 there was 24,000 acres of seagrass, which was a huge increase over the survey before; in 2025 there was 42,000 acres; and that is an 18,000-acre increase in two years. She went on to say what she has seen as she watched it start out in the southern Mosquito Lagoon and then creep over to the northern IRL; last summer there was seagrass all along the shoreline in Titusville; the seagrass work is slowly working its way south, it was above the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Causeway last year, but now it is creeping below the NASA Causeway; the seagrass has not made it down here yet, but it is coming; the SJRWMD did a seed survey a couple of years ago and it found that there are seeds in the sediments all up and down the Lagoon; they just have to keep steady by keeping with the plan, their transect lengths have increases which tells her that the water is getting clearer; the density of the seagrass in the transect is getting denser; everything is pointing towards huge success with the SOIRL Program; and she is hopeful that the Board will keep it going. She concluded by saying at Kelly Park an angler found a Seahorse in his shrimp trap; she knew that there were Seahorses in the norther IRL because the crabbers have been seeing them in their traps for a couple of years now, but to see that one shown up in the central Banana River is good; it shows that it is working; and she hopes that the Board will keep it going.
Keith Winsten, Brevard Zoo Executive Director, stated as elected officials and as County employees, he thinks most of time the Board only hears it when government gets something wrong; this has been sort of a great day hearing how government is getting a lot of things right, from the Fire Chief that was just honored this morning, to the piece about Public Works, and the SOIRL Program is a fantastic example of that; the original Ordinance was well put together; the structure, the oversight, the approval, and the impacts seen step and step again; and the Board has heard it in the Workshops it held in the north and south sides of the County. He reiterated the Board heard it from everybody there, he thinks there was one speaker against, out of 60-plus speakers; he just wants to commend the Board for getting this whole process right, getting the review right, and continuing to act; this is a great government program and all should be proud of that; it involves thousands and thousands of people helping it; he just wanted to recognize the Board today for its role in that and pushing it forward; he knows it is going on the ballot to let the people decide; he is confident what the people will say; he expressed his thanks for giving that chance; and he expressed his thanks for managing such a great program from staff to the Commissioners, they have done a fantastic job with this.
Sandra Sullivan, WAVESaction, stated what she is showing on the overhead projector is of her leaving her community this morning; in 2024, the County stopped spraying the ditches with herbicides; what she is showing drains directly out to the Lagoon; there has not been any seagrass since the law changed in special session of November 2010, that was HB981 to start spraying; she reiterated the County stopped spraying the ditches here, Tropical Trail, US1, and et cetera that drains to the Lagoon; and she posted at the time, she said, “But you want to make a bet, the seagrass is going to make a recovery, and this is being done at a time to show that the Lagoon tax is working.” She stated she is not in favor of the Lagoon tax and one of the things that she wants to talk about is the impact known that the herbicides are a phosphorus that feed algae blooms which kills seagrass; over 90 percent of the seagrass was lost after spraying started; other counties do not have a Lagoon tax, Brevard is the only one with a Lagoon tax, and Brevard has the worst degradation; the County stopped spraying and now it has good recovery starting with the Lagoon; but it is not the Lagoon tax, she calls it the muck tax because she does not know how many people in the room have actually read the Lagoon Plan, but she has. She stated $2 billion worth of muck dredging projects; $600 million worth of stormwater projects at the Cape and Patrick Space Force Base (PSFB); she calls it the military muck tax, because one of the things that is missing in the Lagoon tax is Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substance (PFAS) contamination; but when reading the National Estuary Program (NEP), Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) approved Comprehensive Conservation and Management Plan (CCMP) Brevard is required, as part of the IRL Council to have certain pollutants in the plan, which it does not have; a big one missing is PFAS; and lo and behold in 2010 to 2015, studies were done that muck acts like a sink to attract PFAS. She continued to say then the PSFB came out with its remedial assessment in the beginning of 2015 and back then the Chair was part of a newspaper article, that the muck tax was going to be created, that is what the Chair called it in that newspaper article, and it was said that it is not legal to do it because legislation would have to be changed to create the muck tax to remove muck; it failed twice in appropriations; and she questions whether it is even legal to have the muck tax, they got mucked.
Chair Altman remarked he has no recollection of ever using the term muck tax; and he asked for a copy of that article, because he would love to read it.
Bruce Moia stated the Board is probably surprised to see him because he is not normally here to talk about environmental issues, but this one is important to him; as a Brevard native he has enjoyed this river his whole life; he wants to make sure that it is going to be healthier than what he remembers from when he was young for his grandkids, and their grandkids; this is important and to see the progress that some of the people have talked about brings him joy when he opens up the newspaper and sees an article about how the Lagoon is coming back with seagrasses and Seahorses; it is exciting to read; and he is hopeful for more to come. He stated obviously he is in support of this and he thinks it is needed; if he wanted to see anything different, he would hope that the adjoining counties would also tax themselves, as Brevard does; Brevard cleans up its mess, he wishes they would clean up their mess; maybe to tax more of the people who have been polluting the river for over 60 years, that would be kind of nice; Brevard is getting there one step at a time; and he hopes for the Board to approve this for the ballot.
Commissioner Feltner advised he has a few points for today about other counties and their tax, or the lack of, the fact of the matter is because this sales tax does exist in Brevard County; Brevard has received more support from the State, SJRWMD, and Federal agencies because they are willing to match; it is a much harder conversation when going to Tallahassee and saying, Brevard wants it to spend money here, and they say how much has been raised at home, nothing; that is an impossible ask when going to Tallahassee; and he thinks that is one of the significant benefits of having this at the local level, is getting a lot of additional support for the Lagoon. He mentioned saying this several times, it took three generations to make the river dirty, and he thinks it is going to take this generation to clean it up; he thinks they are partway into it, but progress is being made; a lot of people today came to the two Workshops held and a lot of effort was made to reach out to the community and talking about this; there was great participation in Titusville and in Palm Bay, and he feels like this is the end of a chapter for the County; and the issue will go before the voters and the voters will write the next chapter.
Commissioner Adkinson stated she was put on the SOIRL board and every time she goes to a meeting, she sits there, and it takes her the longest to say all of the progress the Board has made in Brevard County, compared to all of the other board members; she is proud to be able say how much extra money Ms. Barker has received extra, in addition, but only because, as Commissioner Feltner said, Brevard has the money to put up as well to get those extra funds; and she fully-supports allowing the voters to make the decision.
Chair Altman agreed with that; he advised it is a wonderful statement on behalf of Brevard residents and its citizens to show that they care so much for this precious resource and unique treasure that Brevard County has; and he certainly supports putting this back on the ballot.
Morris Richardson, County Attorney, asked for clarity that that included the other two components of the requested action as well, which is approve extension of the existing sales tax use and distribution interlocal agreements with municipalities, subject to voter approval of the sales tax renewal; and approve the ballot language included in the ordinance.
Commissioner Adkinson responded affirmatively, her motion includes all three.
Commissioner Feltner replied and the seconder.
There being no further comments, the Board adopted Ordinance No. 26-06, for voter referendum to renew the one-half cent infrastructure sales tax for the SOIRL Program; approved the extension of the existing sales tax use and distribution Interlocal Agreement (ILA) with municipalities, subject to voter approval of the sales tax renewal; and approved ballot language for the November 3, 2026, General Election.

title: Approval, Ordinance to place a referendum on the November 3, 2026, ballot to renew the ½-cent infrastructure sales tax for the Save Our Indian River Lagoon Program

action_text:
Tom Mulligan, Solid Waste Management Director, stated Item J.2., is concerning the Solid Waste Collection Contract; the contract has an initial seven-year term that runs through September 30, 2027, with a single provision for a three-year extension through September 30, 2030; the current collector, Waste Management, Inc., has requested that extension, and requested a revision to the price adjustments on an annual basis; he is requesting the Board approve one of the following options; option one is to approve legislative intent to consider the three-year extension of the current Solid Waste Collection Contract, authorize advertising a public hearing and notification to property owners of a potential increase to the Non-Ad Valorem Solid Waste Collection Assessment, and hold a public hearing to be scheduled at a future regular meeting to consider approval of the contract extension and associated assessment increase; option two is to authorize Purchasing Services to advertise an Request for Proposal (RFP) to competitively select a solid waste collection provider, authorize the County Manager to establish a Selection and Negotiation Committee, and staff will bring back a negotiated contract for the Board’s consideration; and option three is any other action as determined by the Board.
Rick Heffelfinger stated he thinks that what Sandra Sullivan mentioned is what brought her to this Commission and then she started her little quest to get things straightened out; that is what brought him to the Commission meetings seven years ago; he also has made some recommendations, not necessarily through a Citizen Efficiency and Effectiveness Recommendations (CEER), but through the online page; there are some things that need to be fixed in the Contract and one of those is, somebody else hauling away the County’s stuff; Waste Management has had a monopoly on this, they hold tight reins on recyclables; he does not think there is anybody else who can do recyclables; and if he remembers correctly, it was the County that gave them an incentive to build that facility, it is a wonderful facility, but they own it. He reiterated that he does not think anybody else has a facility; he stated he thinks they are going to get recyclables, unless the County wants to do away with the recycle program, but he does not think it wants to do that; those recyclables taken out of the landfill should extend the landfills, if they are in fact, taken out; maybe the County does not have the greatest participation, but it can work on that; and he thinks the Solid Waste Management Department has worked to do that. He reiterated Waste Management has this monopoly; he stated the last time the County did this contract, there were other bidders, and he said, “Why don’t we go with some of those other bidders, they are cheaper.”; the decision was made by the Commission at that time that it did not have confidence in those bidders, they do not have enough trucks; that is the reason of getting a contract, because when getting a contract, it is a win, and trucks are bought; and if the contract was taken away from somebody else, he bets they are selling trucks. He went on to say if the County breaks the contract up, he realizes that is a pain the butt having to manage potentially three contracts, but the County is paying for the fact that it is being extorted by Waste Management; their service is not good; their service was not good during the last contract; he asked how many people still have piles of debris left over from the frost; the County actually cut them some slack, by giving them a two-week extension and can blow the date given to somebody on the phone, or through one of the requests and giving two weeks; he still has piles of stuff with the grass dying underneath; they are going into hurricane season; he asked where is that all going to go; he stated they are not doing a good job; they do not follow the contract as is; and he knows the Board has that little system where the County can ding them, if enough people complained that they missed a pick up. He added, he made some money last year, and he thinks he has enough people in his neighborhood to say, “Hey, they did not get picked up”; if everybody put their thing in there and they get enough, they get money, he got one of those, but the County does not have any idea how many complaints he had about the way that they leave the garbage can when they are done picking it up; the lid is supposed to closed, nobody seems to be complaining with that; nobody is pushing, the Board manages the Contract, but it does not make any effort to smack them down; he did get one feedback that that was done; but the County needs to break that monopoly.
Sandra Sullivan stated her request today is to go out to bid and do good by the people of Brevard, and go out to a competitive bid because next year they are looking at a 12 percent increase; a 12 percent increase on the taxpayers; from a fiscal perspective doing due diligence and seeing what the County can get as competitive bids would be the rightful thing to do; it is not lost on her the lobbyists that are here, lobbyists that have contributed to the Chair’s campaign, and it will be real interesting whether the Board is fair and equitable by the people of Brevard going out to competitively bid for the best deal; her residents in Wilton Manors, Florida, have switched from Waste Management and other entities have switched from Waste Management; put it out to the competitive process; and just do not do what the lobbyists say, like the Chair’s phone during a vote for the hospital, where the Chair got a text message, “Here’s who to vote for.”
Joanne Stanley, Republic Services, stated Republic Services is a $16 billion environmental services company that picks up solid waste and recycling, is located in 42 states, has 18,000 trucks, and picks up about five million homes a day; Republic Services is a viable option for the County to actually put this out for Request for Proposals (RFP); Republic Services has about a 99.5 percent pick up rate and its services are excellent throughout the State and the country; and she asked for the Board to pick option two and put out an competitive RFP for services.
Jordin Chandler, Government Affairs Manager for Waste Management, stated he is a lifelong resident of Brevard County and a proud constituent of District 5; Waste Management is proud to serve Brevard County, not just as a service provider but as an integral part of the community; there are more than 300 employees who do not just work here, they live here, raise families here, and they show up every single day to serve their neighbors; his team members are in the neighborhoods before sunrise, interacting with residents, helping solve problems, supporting school events, and give back through charitable endeavors all across the community; he can simply say that Waste Management is not just of the community, it is truly in this community making a difference every single day; while Waste Management knows that no service operation is ever perfect, and what defines them is its commitment by working to earn the trust of the community and to grow together every day, he is asking the Board to pursue option one, and consider approval of the three-year renewal that is outlined in the current and existing franchise agreement; this extension would take the contract through September 30, 2030, and after which it will go out for a competitive RFP; this being the only renewal option built in the current contract by providing a structured pathway forward; and Waste Management is asking for the Board to pursue that. He mentioned what is important here, Waste Management services 92,000 households; continuity of service is important and a renewal ensures at this particular point in time zero disruption during a critical time; reliability is what is important here, that the Board can count on; transitioning providers at this particular point in time introduces operational risks, staffing disruption, potential service gaps, and renewal of this current agreement ultimately avoids those risks altogether; what is important here, cost predictability; he thinks staff has done a phenomenal job in outlining the potential fiscal impact that there could be, if this were to go out to a competitive RFP; and an RFP at this particular point in time is due to the market volatility. He concluded by saying this decision today is about certainty versus uncertainty, continuity versus disruption, and a trusted relationship versus transition risk; this renewal keeps a proven system in place, maintains reliability, provides cost stability, and preserves strong community engagement; he asked for the Board at this point in time to consider option one; and he stated in 2030 this will go out to competitive a RFP.
Dean Ulrich, Division Manager for Waste Pro, stated he is a Brevard County resident; Waste Pro is encouraging the Board to put this out for a competitive bid; Waste Pro is nowhere near the size of Waste Management or Republic Services, but is more than qualified and has substantial resources that is enough to do the job; Waste Pro is a Florida-based company that is headquartered in Longwood, is celebrating its 25th year, and is pleased with the growth that goes on in Brevard County; right now in Brevard County, Waste Pro has six municipal contracts; he reiterated they are not as large as the others, but are fully-capable of providing the service for everybody; Waste Pro does operate much larger operations around Brevard County, so the resources are there by having a large division that surrounds Brevard County; they are in Port St. Lucie, Sanford, and Daytona, all the way around Brevard; he reiterated there are plenty of resources for Waste Pro to pull from; and he encourages going out for bid.
Commissioner Adkinson asked what the results are for those other municipalities or counties who have gone out to bid recently.
Mr. Mulligan replied he knows there were three other counties that have gone out to bid recently in 2024; he believes that Lake County ended up with a 42 percent increase on their third renewal of the Contract; Orange County ended up with an 82 percent increase; Volusia County ended up with only a seven percent increase; and the reason why is the difference between whether they have a cost adjustment allowance, or a low cap in the cost adjustment of five percent for annual cost adjustment, and the collector was able to keep up with the Consumer Price Index year to year.
Chair Altman inquired about the municipalities in Brevard County.
Mr. Mulligan replied he is not aware of any of their recent contracts and he believes the City of Cocoa, or it may be the City of Cocoa Beach, that is currently going out for and RFP.
Commissioner Adkinson stated she would like to make a motion to approve option one.
Commissioner Feltner stated he will second.
Chair Altman advised he will be voting against that, he would have preferred option two because he would like to see the Board competitively bid, especially due to the nature of the length of time in the past that the Board did not bid.
The Board approved Option 1, approving legislative intent to consider a three-year extension of the current Solid Waste Collection Contract; authorized advertising of a public hearing and notification to property owners of a potential increase to the Non-Ad Valorem Solid Waste Collection Assessment; and authorized for the public hearing to be scheduled at a future regular meeting to consider approval of the contract extension and associated assessment increases.

action_text:
Morris Richardson, County Attorney, stated staff has discussed with Commissioners, individually before in briefings a situation with Change Healthcare, which was the County’s previous vendor for collecting Emergency Medical Services (EMS) billing for Fire Rescue; they had a data breach that resulted in a long delay in billing; to some extent, it has resulted, even though eventually they resumed billing, and there are some bills that were rejected because they were not properly billing within 90 days and some insurers have a provision to reject; he has been looking at alternatives, once staff is able to fully-evaluate the County’s potential losses resulting from that activity; he has been assessing the County’s remedies through litigation and otherwise; currently, there is a multi-district litigation pending in Minnesota regarding other issues of non-local government providers who were harmed by the state of breach; recently, at a meeting late last week, he learned that there is a movement now for local governments to be included, and perhaps, any prong of that; and he may need some flexibility in June where the Board does not meet to take action, to get the County involved up front, to best preserve its rights, and put the County in the best position to recoup as much as it possibly can. He asked the Board for preliminary authorization now for him to engage class counsel and to take initial steps to participate in that litigation; and he will bring back more information to the Board in July. He advised that he may not need to do this, but he wants to be in the position that if he needs to act quickly in June when the Board is not meeting, that he is able to do that to be in the best position to put the County in a good place to get everything it can.
Commissioner Feltner asked if he wanted that in a motion.
Attorney Richardson responded that would be good if he could get that.
Commissioner Feltner stated he would make that motion.
Commissioner Adkinson stated she will second.
Attorney Richardson advised he will return to the Board with information of what happened.
The Board granted Morris Richardson, County Attorney, preliminary authorization for flexibility in June, if the need arises, to take quick action, to engage class counsel, and take initial steps to participate in litigation against Change Healthcare, to preserve the County’s rights and to be put in the best possible position to recoup as much as possible, resulting from a data breach causing delays in EMS billing for Fire Rescue and ultimately, bills being rejected for not being properly billed within the 90 days; and directed Attorney Richardson to report back to the Board in July with any information.
Upon consensus of the Board, the meeting adjourned at 12:10 p.m.

Chair Altman stated he thinks the Board can have a quick discussion, he does not think it needs to have a separate vote; he thought this was interesting and he had some interesting conversations with staff; they did a really good job in their briefing; the issue came up, something he thinks the Board needs to be aware of; maybe in future meetings or thinking of a future policy; this is a final plat approval, it is in District 4 but he thinks it applies to all Districts, and that is why he pulled it; as the County puts more and more of these developments in, roads and public ownership, the present Municipal Service Taxing Units (MSTUs) are not adequate for the maintenance; the County is digging a hole for itself every time the Board does this; if there is a gate, the streets may be private, so they are maintained by the private developer; but perhaps there needs to be an analysis and see how deep of a hole the County is digging and maybe try to adjust. He mentioned he does not know if it is more private streets or have an MSTU that is adequate to cover, but he thinks these plat approvals come and go, but the Board knows it is building the County in debt situation, or inability to maintain the roads.
Commissioner Feltner asked when the Board is at the plat approval process, can it be designated private roads if they are not behind a gate; is that something that can be done; and he was just wondering for the future, moving forward.
Tad Calkins, Assistant County Manager, responded typically the roadway maintenance is discussed during the preliminary subdivision process; at that point, they could be private but one does not necessarily have to have a gate for the ownership and maintenance of the roadway, but typically they are gated the reason they want the gate; and if they have a gate then they do have to be private. He added they want to have the private road and to be exclusive and where they can limit access to their neighborhood, and that is what they typically do through the development process.
Commissioner Feltner advised that has been his knowledge since being on the Board, that if it is behind a gate that is a pretty good indication that it is private; there is some maintenance with the gates; he lives in a neighborhood like that and it is surprising how much they spend on that; going forward, for these, they do not necessarily have to be behind a gate for them to be private, that is just an agreement early on with the County; and he asked if that is correct.
Mr. Calkins responded affirmatively.
Chair Altman stated those were good questions.
Commissioner Adkinson stated she does not want to pull anything, she just wanted to make a comment on F.19. and F.21.

Rick Heffelfinger stated this one was an interesting one; this is all about an as is deed for the Board where there was a problem with a pumping station, he believes, and the fence was 30 feet too close to the County or it was giving up 30 feet; his question was he thought it always went through zoning and all that stuff, pull permits, but somebody built a screen room four inches away from the property line; he does not know how that got through; he asked if the County installed the fence in the wrong place or if that was the homeowner's fence, it is not clear; he commented he is a little concerned that the County does all this stuff with permitting, one is supposed to have a plot plan; he does not know who screwed that up, but the County was very, very nice and they sold that piece of property so the guy would still have he thinks three feet so he could go beside his screen room; he thinks that was nice, but he questioned how the County got in that situation in the first place; and he does not know if there was any corrective action where the County needs to look at what it is doing with permitting. He noted either the County screwed up and put the fence in the wrong place, the homeowner assumed that is where it was, and then the homeowner pulled the screen room permit, did not pull his own survey, and ended up going into the easement; he is just trying to find out why that happened, although the County made $332 by selling that little plot, so that was revenue; but he did not know if anybody wanted to look at that and figure out why that happened.
Chair Altman stated he will go through all of them and then answer.
Commissioner Feltner advised he could answer this really fast; this is a lift station; it is in Indian Harbor Beach, but a County facility; Indian Harbor Beach would have issued the permit, so the County is working with the homeowner as they do not want him to have to take down fences, and he thinks they have a pool, et cetera; and therefore, for $300 the County was able to get this fixed.
Mr. Heffelfinger stated if one is going to move the fence, he understands, but it is not going to move it all the way as far as they could, so the County is going to sell them that little piece.
Commissioner Feltner noted he thinks that is right, it is about three feet.
Mr. Heffelfinger interjected by saying that would have been an Indian Harbor Beach zoning or planning, permitting.
Commissioner Feltner commented he thinks it is just a permit issue.
Mr. Heffelfinger asked who owned the fence, did the County own the fence.
Commissioner Feltner replied no, he thinks it is their fence.
Mr. Heffelfinger commented, oh, they tried to steal the County’s property then.
Commissioner Feltner explained staff is working with the homeowner.
Mr. Heffelfinger stated well the homeowner should not have put that fence there, so he does not know why they were allowed to; and again, he just does not know if somebody’s going to give a heads up to that district that they did not permit that very well.
Chair Altman stated the Board can get him a meeting schedule for Indian Harbor Beach if he wants to go.
Mr. Heffelfinger stated he does not want to go, he just figured when the County gets caught in a situation like that, that it should be asked how they let that fence get put there 30 feet on the County’s property.

action_text: Rick Heffelfinger stated this is an interesting one; it is about an emergency purchase order; this is Utility Services again; there was a problem with the front side of the water processing facility, the headwater, odor control, and structural assessment; he pulled all the reports because this is an emergency and he wanted to see what this emergency was; water is a hot topic these days; he pulled the report by Black and Veatch who were called in to do a report; there is an annotation in that report that says the first indication of this problem was 2021; he does not know if that was a typo or when Veatch was brought in, but that was only two years after this water plant was updated; and the liner was coming off inside. He went on to say from 2021, then in 2024 they came in, took pictures, they had before and after, and then again in 2026; by the time they get into 2026, it is an emergency and it is going to cost the County a lot, $1,130,635 as an emergency; he thinks the County skipped the multiple bidders because this has to happen sooner rather than later because it is an emergency; and he was wondering if the County had dropped the ball. He noted he would have thought two years after something was built, the County would be able to get a warranty claim on that because somebody built it wrong and the evidence is somebody went back through the notes and said the liner was improperly applied; this was a manufacturer or installer defect; he does not know why, if it was actually detected in 2021, why it took until 2026 and became an emergency because it is quite clear in here; he thinks everybody knows hydrogen sulfide gas produced by part of the leachate that is in it and the nasty stuff that is in the processing water, it creates hydrogen sulfide, which is why the odor detection system is put in; the stuff is also colorless, corrosive, toxic, and flammable; and they measured readings that were way too high which has probably helped along with the liner. He noted he just does not know how the County got here into an emergency when it looks to him that the thing was breaking down in 2021 and it was only two years old; right now it is only seven years old; it is a big project and they are talking about it actually says that the secondary system is not even working at all now; he would guess water is still going through it, but he does not know, maybe it is not screening anything; that concerns him because it appears like staff did not catch that or it did catch it because the report says it was updated, but he does not know when it was originally done, but if it was in 2021, then he would have thought all those warnings would have been there; and that is all he has on that one.
