action_text:
Richard Heffelfinger stated this sounds like a public hearing to amend the Barefoot Bay Utility Services rates; there were some people here last month that he thinks were quite adamant that the Board needs to give them some relief; he does not know if this gives them 100 percent relief, but it is good news; it is going to reduce their rate back at least to last year, so he thinks that is good; there is a fiscal impact, it does not say there is; and when it rolls back to 2025, he guesses there was a study that was done that identified that phasing out of the Barefoot Bay was not going to cost that high of a rate, because all of those monies that were being collected, partially because of that rate, he thinks was to maintain that plant. He went on to say he hopes the Board just keeps it on its last legs until it phases out; it does not say how much revenue is being lost due to that rollback; again, that is probably an enterprise fun thing, and does he care; he does not know, it just seemed like a reducing rates and not showing how much rate loss there was; and he was just a little bit concerned about that.
Chair Altman stated why the Board does not do this, if Mr. Heffelfinger is finished, there are 11 cards on this Item, maybe have staff give a quick summary of it; maybe some of the questions could be answered; and a lot of people showed up from Barefoot Bay to be heard.
Mr. Heffelfinger stated he thinks there was a multi-year rate increase that everybody was squawking, he does not know what it rolled all that back; and he thinks that was almost complete or did complete last year.
Chair Altman stated to let the staff give a presentation.
Edward Fontanin, Utility Services Director, explained at the last Board meeting, the Board approved for the Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer District to be sunset, effective in January 2030; that is based on the last bond payment associated with Barefoot Bay being made in December 2029; and when staff does rate calculations, they are always looking at read calculations for the entity to be around for perpetuity.
Chair Altman asked if everybody can hear.
Mr. Fontanin asked if he should start over.
Chair Altman replied yes.
Mr. Fontanin reiterated the last Board meeting, the Board approved for the Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer District to be sunset in January 2030; the rationale of that is that the last bond payment associated with the Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer District occurs in December 2029; based on that Board action, staff looked at, along with the rate consultant, an analysis of looking at what the needed revenue would be in order to sustain itself until the 2030 sunset period; based on that, they did an analysis, they reviewed that the user rates could be rolled back to 2025, he believes that is a reduction of 4.8 percent; and they would flat line them there out. He noted in the Agenda Report, there are further redlines associated with it, so anytime a revision is made to a Resolution, it has to be shown through a red line process; when the rates were approved in 2022, the rates that are shown in redline, not only are they adjusted but basically they were shown to the 2025 rate, and the remaining rates they just made current from the 2022 to the 2026; in a nutshell, water and sewer user rates rolled back to 2025, at a 4.8 percent reduction; and they will be flat lined through 2030; come 2030, the Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer accounts in the Water and Sewer District will get turned over to adopted to whatever the Countywide system is at that time.
Chair Altman advised this is not passing the rate, this is simply to advertise.
Mr. Fontanin stated that is correct, this is step one.
Commissioner Adkinson stated when she had people coming into her office saying the rates in Barefoot Bay are difficult; and she asked when the Board asked Mr. Fontanin to look at this, what did he anticipate the percentage rate increase being over the next three years prior to his relooking at it.
Mr. Fontanin responded by Board direction, staff used the Consumer Price Index (CPI) water and sewer maintenance index, so the last adjustment was 4.8 percent; and they look at it every November.
Commissioner Adkinson asked what they anticipated those increases to be.
Mr. Fontanin replied he would have to look at the number, but the way everything is going, he would anticipate another four or five percent increase.
Commissioner Adkinson inquired doing what the County is doing, if it is not only rolling it back, it is stopping those increases for the next three years.
Mr. Fontanin replied affirmatively; he stated if he is being asked him the way everything is going in the industry, the CPI is absolutely in a trajectory to keep going up; and Commissioner Adkinson is correct, they are kind of like flat lining it.
Dennis LaBelle commented he is here representing the unified group of Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer customers; they are here to address a clear legal contradiction in how Brevard County structures its water billing; it is specifically this Agenda Item; today the Board is voting on a proposal to decrease their water and sewer rates to the 2025 level, a 5.15 percent decrease; while any rate reduction is a step in the right direction, let them be clear that this tiny rollback is an inadequate Band-Aid that does nothing to alleviate the crushing weight of their bills; and it will not placate them. He pointed out for everyone who is watching, his bill is $110 for two people, and to compare that to his or her bills; between 2022 and 2026 Barefoot Bay Utility rates skyrocketed by a staggering 54 percent and rolling rates back by just one year leaves residents trapped under a compounding, massive financial penalty compared to the rest of Brevard County customers the County manages; a single-family residential home in Barefoot Bay is in an exact same consumer class as residential homes in Port St. John, Merritt Island, and Mims; and they flush the same water, require the same statutory environmental processing, and answer to the same Board of County Commissioners. He stated basically, a 54 percent increase rollback of 5.515 percent is not adequate; when they turned over the system, Barefoot Bay system, to the County, they were required to pay a fee; when new builders build these massive buildings; he asked if they are required to pay a fee to hook up; he stated it is just for my information; and he asked if he has to pay like $5 million to hook up to the system.
Chair Altman responded yes, there is an impact fee that new construction has to pay; and he asked staff to give a general idea of maybe where that is.
Mr. LaBelle asked if it is like $5 million or $10 million for $10,000 units.
Mr. Fontanin stated it is under a thousand dollars for water and sewer, and the exact amount he believes is about $700 or $800.
Mr. LaBelle asked if it was per toilet.
Mr. Fontanin replied per Equivalent Residential Connection (ERC), a single-family home equivalent.
Mr. LaBelle asked if for Barefoot Bay it would be $5,000.
Mr. Fontanin responded it is a calculation, so as he will see, they do the same calculation, so the Agenda Item will be later about the connection fees for Countywide; it starts off with a two-bedroom equivalent; and then staff uses the Administrative Code to do the calculation on anything that alters from that, whether it is higher or lower.
Chair Altman mentioned he appreciated Mr. LaBelle’s input; the Board is not voting on anything today other than advertising the ordinance, so it is not going to do any fees or increases; and this is only to have permission to advertise.
Denise Emmel stated she has a single-family home in Barefoot Bay, and her water bill is $94; she is the only one who lives there; she will not even power wash her house because of the water bill; despite the facts of their sameness, the County continues to carve Barefoot Bay Utilities customers out into an isolated billing island; even with this 5.15 percent decrease, their neighbors across the County will still pay a base sewer fee of $32.79, while they are charged a premium $54; and their consumption rate will remain highly inflated. She went on to say this is not a difference in usage, it is a geographical penalty; freezing or slightly rolling back these rates until 2029 does not solve the underlying injustice, only integrating them into the Countywide system sooner will truly help with their bills; all five of the Commissioners are equal in representing them and in being responsible for their water and wastewater; since buying their utility system 26 years ago, the customers have paid inflated rates; and she asked if 26 years long enough, must they wait another three and a half years to see real relief. She asked the Commission to stop delaying and integrate them into a single, equal County utility class immediately.
Karen Conrad remarked she would like to closely look at the administrative logic the County uses to justify the residents’ utility bills; Brevard County Utility Services is currently operating six wastewater treatment plants for five of those plants; the County operates a unified regional pricing structure; this means if a plant in Northern Brevard needs a multi-million dollar upgrade or a facility in the South Beaches faces high operational costs, these financial burdens are socialized across the entire County footprint; and the County does this because it recognizes that a unified utility network benefits the whole region’s health, ecology, and economy. She continued by saying when it comes to the sixth plant, their plant, Barefoot Bay, the logic just flips; suddenly, regional socialization stops and localized billing begins; and she asked why this principle of a shared infrastructure applies to only five plants, but ends at the borders of Barefoot Bay.
Chuck Barnett stated they have heard the response that the County’s hands are tied until existing utility bonds are paid off on December 31, 2029; respectfully, Commissioners, this is a bureaucratic excuse, not a legal barrier; bond obligations do not prevent the County from giving them operational equity today; it could vote to integrate Barefoot Bay into the Countywide system now by keeping the remaining bond payments as a transparent, temporary fix line item exclusively on Barefoot Bay’s bills until 2029; the existing debt will still be paid by the users of the system, and not one penny needs to be paid by other customers; and if current bond debt obligations does not prevent the County from blending rates from the rest of its system, it cannot be used as an excuse to isolate them. He noted the dual standard is administratively inconsistent; if this system is regional for five plants, it must be reasonable for all six; this is something the Board agreed to when it voted two weeks ago to integrate Barefoot Bay into the Countywide system; and it has no legal or logical basis to justify waiting until December 31, 2029.
Bonnie Carpenter commented she lived in the Pines for 23 years, now she lives in, and is a resident of, Barefoot Bay; she is here to challenge the accounting behind Barefoot Bay’s inflated utility rates; when a municipality isolates a single infrastructure asset for localized billing, the math almost always penalizes the captive ratepayer through the over allocation of the administrative overhead; they are paying a massive premium on their base facility charges; and she pays $110 a month, and she throws her dishwater out on her plants, so she does not get it. She mentioned they want to know exactly how much Central County overhead is being packed into that number; their billing is processed centrally by Brevard County Utility Services; their engineering is managed centrally; the executive legal teams and administrative staff are all located in Viera, funded by general utility revenues; and if they are paying higher rates to cover localized operational costs, but they are also being charged a percentage to support the County’s Central administrative apparatus, they are being double dipped.
Norman Perkins stated they are publicly requesting a transparent line item of the most recent cost service study; they want proof that revenues collected by Barefoot Bay are staying entirely within their plant ecosystem, and are not actively subsidizing central staff or capital improvements of the other five blended facilities; in addition, they are publicly requesting a transparent line item audit going back to their utility increases from 2013, Resolution No. 13-002, and a transparent line item audit of increases from 2022, Resolution No. 22-001; and they want proof that the revenue collected from Barefoot Bay customers has been used for, and accounted for, the items in areas that were stated in the Resolutions that they were used. He explained his water bill was $186 last month, and it is unfortunate that he cannot even drink the water; he has a whole house filter system, which many people in Barefoot Bay also cannot drink the water there; they either buy the water, use it like that, or they have to have some kind of a filtration system; and it is unfortunate that he pays $186 and cannot even drink the water.
Ray Delorme stated he wants to bring this back to the human costs of this rate structure; the vast majority of the customers that use Barefoot Bay water and sewer system live in two manufactured home communities; a majority of these residents are retirees, Veterans, and individuals living on fixed social security incomes; their public utility designs are supposed to act as a form of social insurance; and it is meant to protect vulnerable populations from being financially wiped out by localized geographic or infrastructure challenges. He continued by saying over the last few years, while general County utility rate increases were managed at single digit percentages; Barefoot Bay was hit with compounding double digit annual increases; for someone on fixed income at $54 base rate just for wastewater is not just a minor inconvenience, it cuts directly into money needed for groceries, health care, gas, and insurance; he showed the Board a copy of his utility bill as an example of the unfairness; he noted on June 10 to July 10, 2026, the total current charges for 2,800 gallons of usage is $132; with rollback to the 2025 rates, the cost of this bill would be $125; and if this home was on Merritt Island, or another Countywide system, the cost would be $77, big difference. He stated the increase to the other Countywide customers, if the County integrated Barefoot Bay into the Countywide system, now would be $2 a month, or even less if the Barefoot Bay customers continue paying off existing bond debt, as they have proposed; again, he has been there since 2019 when they first moved there, their bill was $46 minimum that they had to pay; his last bill was $143; he asked where does the County go from $46 to $143; and he stated maybe the Board to figure that out and correct that for them.
Terry Brewer commented he has been a Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer District customer for over 12 years; they are a captive consumer class, they cannot choose another sewer provider, they cannot dig their own septic tanks, and they are entirely at the mercy of this Board; forcing a fixed income retirement community to bear 100 percent of its localized infrastructure burden for another three and one-half years, while younger, wealthier, more developing parts of the County enjoy socialized blended rates is funnily unfair, it is unjust; it is fundamentally unaffordable for many of the residents in this system, including mobile home communities of Barefoot Bay and Snug Harbor; and they have been paying a lot more than everyone else in the County. He went on to say since the first double digit increases of 2022; they are not asking for a refund; and they just want the County to stop fleecing them.
Sydne James mentioned to wrap up their group’s presentation today, they want to look forward to the solution; they acknowledge that the County Commission has previously discussed and voted to move forward to sunset the independent Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer District, and by advertising today to roll back rates a tiny bit and promise they will not increase from now until they are integrated into the Countywide system; this is not a gift, she read the audit, they were overpaying and the audit said that, so the County gets to not raise it anymore and roll it back; and they are still paying on everything they owe on. She reiterated it is not a gift to charge them more; in fact, legally the County is not supposed to charge more than is required; these are tiny concessions the County is offering, and they do not solve the problem of the unfair and unaffordable rates for Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer customers; let them address the claim that this transition cannot happen until December 31, 2029, because of outstanding bond debt; this is legally incorrect; Florida law allows this Board to dissolve the District immediately; the County Attorney can tell the Board as much; the bond holders only care that their debt service is secured by the utilities revenue; and the County does not need to wait three and one-half more years, it can dissolve the District now, absorb Barefoot Bay into the unified County network, and immediately lower their base sewer rate from $54.28 to the Countywide standard of $32.79, or less, depending on the tier of customers. She stated to honor the remaining bond obligations simply place, as previously stated, a transparent, temporary debt service surcharge as a separate line item exclusively on the Barefoot Bay customer bills; this allows them to pay off their outstanding bond debt without being forced to suffer under unaffordable fees for the next three and one-half years; she asked the Board not to let this transition drag out through years of artificial bureaucratic delay; she noted they have stated the legal inconsistency, the mathematical and unfairness, and the clear path to an immediate financial compromise; the Board has the ability to reconsider or repeal its vote from two weeks ago and update the timeline for integration of their utility system; and they ask for a concrete timeline and an expedited vote to finally bring regional utility equity to Barefoot Bay by the end of 2026.
John Requa provided the Board with a handout; he stated he agrees with his fellow residents, and it is nice to see them here; Barefoot Bay is a wonderful place to live, except for the water; that is why they are fighting so hard, they love it there; what he has provided the Board, he asked for this via email and he has come here he does not know how many times that Commissioner Adkinson had this done by the council for going over the prices, the cost, the debt, and everything, the Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer; he read it twice, and he understands a little; the Board will see some questions on its page, and they are for Mr. Fontanin, Commissioner Adkinson, and someone from the council that did this survey; and they are requesting that the Commission comes to Barefoot Bay, send appointment out with the Board of Trustees, it has been done before with a town hall meeting, and explain the audit as it is difficult to understand. He pointed out as an example, there will be questions that he has; he has more as he reads it; but one cannot get it will the three minutes of democracy that it has; he is confused about the cost of the bond when it started, how many bonds were involved, he heard there were at least two, he is confused about how much is collected; the highlighted stuff the Board sees on the pages are answers he received from the audit, he put that on there; he sees the total take in per year is $7,760,587; it is hard looking at that, and he wants to know where the money goes; he would still like to know what the estimated cost is for the consumer when the County goes on the new plan, it has to have an idea of what that is going to be; and there cannot be a forecast unless the County knows what it is going to charge. He mentioned he wants to make sure that none of their funds or what they are paying now are going towards that new facility, since they are going to be liberated and be a part of Brevard County, which they do not feel like they are right now; a separate district is what he keeps hearing; that is his request; he agrees with his fellow citizens; this is amazing, he used to come by himself a couple of years, and this is just heart lifting; he really would like the County to get in touch with the Trustees and set a meeting up; he is requesting that very strongly; there is nothing wrong with transparency, there is nothing wrong with answering questions; and they still disagree with the decision the County made, but it does not mean the questions cannot be answered.
Mr. Heffelfinger advised he would like to come back up because the Board cut him off.
Commissioner Adkinson advised he did not get cut off.
Mr. Heffelfinger asked if he did not get his three minutes, and he wants to play back the tape.
Commissioner Adkinson stated she will make sure the questions will get answered if they have not gotten answered.

action_text:
Brad Molander commented he is an Artificial Intelligence (AI) engineer during the day and he volunteers at Brevard Soccer Academy in the evenings; the reason why he is here tonight, he does not want to take up too much time, but with the property tax on the agenda for this fall and its potential ramifications to the County, he was curious on what modeling had been done for impacts to Parks and Recreation; he noticed the County had some numbers created, and he was wondering if staff has had a plan on the Parks and Recreation side on how that might impact the youth programs; as a reminder, he got into this by one day showing up at his daughter’s soccer practice, and they say, “Hey, we need a coach”, so one volunteers and does it; and he kind of got sucked into the whole thing because when he was little he was in youth soccer and it kind of gave him the opportunities that he has in his life. He went on to say one of the great things about Brevard Soccer Association (BSA) specifically, and other area clubs, is that they are a non-profit organization, so they are here exclusively for the community, to get kids off of iPads, get them outside; as of last spring, they have 1,600 kids in their program; one of the things they are looking at is how those services potentially could impact the club, the parks, but also the families; they have a lot of kids that they subsidize that cannot afford to play soccer; they get them in the club, put them on the field, get them shoes, and get them out there; it is a sight to see if any of the Commissioners are ever near Max Road in the evenings in the fall or spring semester, he or she will see a lot of kids out there having the time of their lives; and that is all due to the volunteers that do it. He expressed his appreciation for all that Parks and Recreation has done for the club up to this point, it has been wonderful; he noted it is a great partnership that they have; that is his root question, what modeling has been done, what impacts are there, and is Parks and Recreation open to talking with some of the area clubs so they could start making provisions to help understand what those impacts could be; their season runs starting right now and goes through right at the end of November; and in February, they fire up again. He expressed his appreciation to the Board for everything it does do in the day in and day out.
Jim Liesenfelt, County Manager, stated he is looking at Ian Golden, Parks and Recreation Director, so he is going to catch Mr. Molander; he will highlight that $18 million number, that is $11 million of General Fund that would not be eligible because it is not a core service, and that $7 million number is the reduction due to less taxable values in the Multiple Services Taxing Units (MSTUs); there are three or four, he forgets the exact number, of park MSTUs; and each part of the County is a little bit different.
Mr. Golden explained the quick answer is if someone requests information, some factual information about what the potential impacts are, they can have a conversation; there is that State law that restricts County employees while they are on the clock from starting conversations; he will not take a position one way or the other, but he will be happy to have a conversation with him; and he was going to catch him on the way out and basically tell him the same thing.
Mr. Molander stated again, it is just a reminder, he guesses it will be helpful; there are a lot of area clubs like theirs, they are not even the largest one, 1,600 kids is a lot of kids; and he thinks it would be helpful to open those lines of communication so they can help work with the parents, because they are getting questions as well.
Commissioner Pritchett stated she feels his pain, and she has a lot of concern, too; and she asked if the Board is allowed to, if this gets implemented next year, to have new voter-approved referendums just for Parks.
Mr. Liesenfelt responded the short answer is any new referendum would have to be at a general election, so that would push it to 2028; and it would not be able to help the first year of reduction.
Commissioner Pritchett explained she does agree with Chair Altman on this, they are taking a lot of this out on the kids, and she has great concern for that herself.
Chair Altman commented those are very good questions, and as County goes through this, hopefully it will have more answers; the problem staff has is they are under the gun; if they try to answer a question, then they are going to be accused of advocating for or against the referendum, so they have to be careful; he really appreciates his question, because if the public is asking for a question, the Board is not preempting he or she prior to having a question; it should have the ability to answer objective questions, how much money, how much is lost, and how does the County replace that; those questions are really good; and he asked the public to please keep them coming.
Sandra Sullivan mentioned she runs a group called Waves Action, and the focus is on accountability and transparency; she has a couple of comments on Amendment 3 on this referendum; coming into this budget time, she and others ask that the Board does some cutting costs of wasteful spending; the sentiment that she has seen on Waves Action are people are pissed off that the spending keeps going up without restraint; the County has the highest assessments, the highest growth, and it has a lot of growth revenue coming in; and the budget went from $1.83 million in 2022 to $2.83 million in 2025, a pretty substantial increase. She stated she is going to just say her disappointment in the last meeting with Commissioner Pritchett coming on this Board; the motion that was taken on the budget to bust the cap, with Commissioner Feltner voting for that, the only no vote was former Commissioner Delaney, to direct staff, and Commissioner Feltner asked staff to clarify if they were preparing two budgets; one to put up there that was not busting the cap, and one not to bust the cap; no, it was clarified they were only preparing a budget to bust the cap; in the last meeting a budget was put up that did not bust the cap, and then at the last minute Chair Altman takes a vote on a different budget with no accountability and transparency, no documents online, and the vote was taken to bust the cap; and she reiterated she is not too happy about that. She pointed out that in coming here for many years there has been the request to cut the Community Redevelopment Agencies (CRAs) that had no debt; no, the County gave $12.1 million to a friend who wants to build through a CRA to build a hotel parking lot, parking building; it did not take action on impact fees; it kicked the can down the road on that; it did not cut waste; she advised the Board do not vote to put Save Our Indian River Lagoon (SOIRL) on because it may need this if this Amendment 3 passes for infrastructure needs; no, the Board went ahead and put that on there; she hopes people vote no; she asked the Board at this time to go and look at that budget, cut waste, cut costs, and cut where it needs to; Commissioner Atkinson did a very good list of things that could be cut; there is a lot of wasteful spending; and it is time to take action on that now before this budget goes through or the County is just digging itself deeper.

Chair Altman called for a public hearing to consider a resolution adjusting connection fees for South Beaches, Merritt Island, North Brevard, Port St. John, and the South Central Mainland Service Area.
Edward Fontanin, Utility Services Director, stated Item H.1. is to amend the Utility Services Rate Resolution adjusting connection fees for South Beaches, Merritt Island, North Brevard, Port St. John, and the South Central Mainland Service Area; as the Board can see in the Agenda Item a clean version and a red line version; to just go over the redline version, the core of it is that staff made the adjustments to the connection fee to get current from the 1993 to current; in addition, they also took the liberty of doing some definition revisions; some of the small service fees like towing service; they made some minor adjustments from like $50 to $75, and of that magnitude; but the big component with regard to this is the water sewer connection fee and seeking approval.
Richard Heffelfinger commented the County did a big blow up on 7-7-26; he was really pissed off on 7-7-26, because this was extremely confusing; he will give Mr. Fontanin and his gang credit, the attachments were cleaned up quite nicely; there are no more dock files, no more confusion that this was only connection fees; what he would have loved to have had the first time was this, this study right here would have caused that confusion to go away; he asked why it is left only at the public hearing, because the public cannot study it, he does not know; and if he was a conspiracy theorist, he would say the County held out until the end. He went on to say this study was conducted on October 22, 2025, and it should have been attached at the time that conversation was had; the County wasted a lot of his time and its own he thinks; he thinks it was not a clean . . . and he is glad to see it cleaned up, and he will give Mr. Fontanin credit for that; he would hope his complaining would have had something to do with that, maybe, maybe not, but he will take that; and this is connection fees and to jam it to them, he is 100 percent in favor.
Commissioner Pritchett advised she did not get the privilege of working through this with the rest of the Commission, so she is not going to vote to support this; she would have supported spreading it out over a five-year period of time to just check and see how much it might have maybe knocked the County out of the market of new housing; and she is just letting the Board know this, that is going to be her vote.
Chair Altman asked if there is a motion.
Commissioner Feltner stated he is waiting to see what the Commission is going to do here; and maybe there is more discussion needed.
Commissioner Adkinson noted as Mr. Heffelfinger said, staff cleaned it up; a lot of work was done on it, staff took a lot of time; she is ready to support this thing because of the work that they have done; and she supports connection fees on new builds.
There being no further comments or objections, the Board adopted Resolution No. 26-063, amending the Utility Services Rate Resolution encompassing South Beaches, Merritt Island, North Brevard, Port St. John, and the South Central Mainland Service Area, adjusting the fees once from the current fees to the full amount of the recommended connection fees, to be implemented on October 1, 2026.

action_text:
Chair Altman called for a public hearing to consider an ordinance amending Chapter 102, Article IV, Division 3 of the Brevard County Code to make data centers ineligible for Economic Development Ad Valorem Tax Exemptions.
Morris Richardson, County Attorney, explained Item H.2. is an ordinance amending Chapter 102, Article IV, Division 3 of the Brevard County Code to make data centers ineligible for economic development ad valorem tax exemptions; at the April 7, 2026, regular meeting, the Board approved legislative intent and permission to advertise an ordinance to make data centers ineligible for those tax exemptions; that was approved at the time; it took a while because of a previous amendment to the Code that had not been incorporated by Municode into the County’s codified ordinances, so had to take some measures to make sure that this is codified correctly if the Board enacts it, but it is before the Board tonight; and the proposed ordinance provides a definition for the term data center, which is drawn from Federal and State law, further provides the data centers are ineligible for the economic development ad valorem tax exemption program.
Richard Heffelfinger remarked this has been hanging out since April, so he is glad to finally see it show up; the fiscal impact is an interesting statement, because it says the correlation is that the lack of incentive may cause the developer to locate to another Florida county or state; Brevard County will receive no new ad valorem and tangible personal property tax revenues from this project; that was exactly the objective of doing this was to give them no reason to want to come here; people have heard all of the news, it is a hot topic, it is a hot thing for everybody; and there may be a big boom at the construction phase, but then the County would eat it on the water, the electricity usage, and the public’s going to bear a large part of that. He mentioned he does not think that is disputed, he thinks that is fact now; the Chinese is going to beat the US at Artificial Intelligence (AI), he doubts it; that is just not something that he thinks as a taxpayer and as a resident here that he does not want to bear that cost, and he does not think anybody does; they can be stuck out in the middle of nowhere where there is plenty of water; the County does not have plenty of water; people know that, they have been telling that for years, and yet, the County is still building like crazy, but that is a different topic; he asked if Brevard has one nuclear power plant; and it should get some more if it wants to play with data centers, so he thinks the intent here was good, but the intent is not complete. He noted the Board is going to hear some requests for a motion to ask for a moratorium, they have more time to look at it, because he does want to . . . they say that these things are fact; he asked are they truly facts; what is the water; he stated the Board should hear some people say, no, man, they fill up the chillers and they reuse the water, so they are not really a big water drain; but that is not . . . he heard that one place, he does not know if it is true or not; time to think about it would be good time to spend; since they are probably not going to want to come here; and to say the County is going to write them off completely, that is not fair either, but he does not want to incentivize them. He pointed out a moratorium would allow this issue to be settled and studied better to decide exactly what the impacts are; that is a good way to put that on hold and have more data come together, because a lot of people are digging it and there are going to be technology changes; maybe some of this heat factor, electronics incredible jumps and bounds; the County is doing now what it could not, unthinkable 10 years ago; maybe that data center problem goes away, and maybe Brevard could have data centers; until that happens, sometime needs to be spent to think about it; and he would like to see a move for a motion to have a moratorium, bring back an ordinance language for that, so more time can be spent on this before somebody drops a big problem in the County’s lap.
Chair Altman asked before Mr. Heffelfinger leaves, if under Senate Bill 180 is the County allowed to pass a moratorium; he was under the impression that . . .
Attorney Richardson advised it could be problematic with regard to Senate Bill 180.
Chair Altman stated the Board can get an opinion for that later, but it is one of the . . .
Mr. Heffelfinger interrupted by saying no a motion, take a motion to look at it would be a good start.
Sandra Sullivan expressed her appreciation to the Board for putting this on the Agenda to remove the data center tax exemption for the Economic Development Commission (EDC) tax abatement; the citizens are also asking for a two-year moratorium on hyperscale data centers; yesterday, Flagler County and Lakeland passed moratoriums on data centers, while Edgewater passed a permanent ban; Ormond Beach votes tonight, and Palm Beach and Dixie County meeting on August 6th; there are about 20 counties and cities Florida wide; in advance of that, she spoke at the last meeting, that have a moratorium; as the Board knows, the Governor race has really heated up over this issue; and she wants to just go over a little bit about the past performance on this particular issue. She went on to say Brevard County voted to approve the legislative intent on April 7th; Brevard did not go to legislative intent before the vote on December 17th, which gave the data centers 20-year tax exemption under Florida Statute 196.1995; Brevard County voters passed the referendum on November 5, 2024; they voted for specific, strictly bound constitutional authority; the Statute dictates any ad valorem tax exemption granted by the County Board under this program cannot exceed 10 years; and it should not have been approved in the first place. She stated on November 5, 2024, when voters approved the tax exemption abatement, voters would probably not have voted for it if the Board had put in a 20-year tax exemption on data centers; right after on December 17, 2024, right before Christmas when everybody is busy, when former Commissioner Feltner was on the EDC board and Chair of this Commission; the Ordinance was changed for a 20-year tax exemption; as established by Florida Statute 125.66, an ordinance cannot be changed without going out for legislative intent, as the Board did for this Item, for voter-referendum; she came here and spoke about this; and she is grateful that the Board has taken action on this. She stated data centers concern the public very much, the hyperscale; she hopes the Board will consider also doing a moratorium; two years, not a long time, but enough time to evaluate; her understanding is the EDC has some proposals in front of them; as the Board knows, the EDC gets a 12-month exemption on public records by the law that the State has done; they do not even get to find out what is really going on, but they know what is going on because she has done enough records requests to see that the EDC is already working on this issue; and she hopes the Board will approve this Item today and correct that record.
Steve Burdett stated in his retirement, he has kind of had a lot of time to see what is going on with these data centers throughout the country, and he knows a lot of people have had concerns over basically what happens to the water availability, what happens with their utility bills, and the same with electricity; he is especially concerned about the noise, especially for those who have to live by these things; and he knows from his experience, he believes the County has a Noise Ordinance, but he is not sure how it applies to a business of this nature. He continued by saying the other concern he expressed, and this was even before a lot of these data centers were built, was, and this was more at the national level, not necessarily the Board, but what happens to these data centers, the County has these redevelopment areas that were supposed to be used to take care of blight; he asked if these data centers ends up becoming outdated, who is going to take them down, who is going to get rid of them, and are they going to be an eyesore; is that part of these people have to do when they decide to build these data centers; and he reiterated he just wanted to express his concerns. He mentioned he knows a lot of people throughout the country have had concerns about it, and he would just assume they do not start here, or if they do that the County makes sure that they are governed properly.
Commissioner Pritchett stated she wanted to make a motion to approve; and Commissioner Feltner seconded the motion.
Attorney Richardson stated the Agenda is phrased as ‘consider adopting’, and he asked if the Board would mind phrasing that in just a, adopt the proposed ordinance, is that the motion.
Commissioner Pritchett responded affirmatively.
There being no further comments or objections, the Board adopted Ordinance No. 26-11, pertaining to the Brevard County Economic Development Ad Valorem Tax Exemption Program; amending Chapter 102 – Taxation, Article IV – Ad Valorem Property Taxation, Division 3; Economic Development Ad Valorem Tax Exemption Ordinance, Brevard County Code of Ordinances; amending Section 102-184 – Definition of Terms; amending Section 102-185 – Economic Development Ad Valorem Tax Exemption Established; providing for resolution of conflicting provisions; providing for severability; providing for an area encompassed; providing for an effective date; and providing for inclusion in the Code of Ordinances.

action_text:
Kathy Wall, Central Services Director, tonight the Board is here to discuss State Lobbying Services, and Steve Crisafulli is here to discuss his annual report.
Steve Crisafulli, representing SBM Partners, stated as the Agenda says, it is about the State lobbying contract, but it was never discussed regarding the legislative session; they discussed potentially doing that in July; and he expressed his appreciation to the Board for its grace in allowing them to do it at this meeting. He went on to say in a nutshell, he sent each of the Commissioners a breakdown of the legislative session; if he or she did not get it from him, maybe Ms. Wall or the County Manager sent that to the Commissioners; this year was the early session year where session starts in January, finishes in March, and yet again, this year they finished the session without a budget; the Governor called the Legislature back in session in the middle of May to work on a budget; at that time, after a little over two weeks, they were able to pass $117.5 billion budget, which is one-half of a billion dollars less than what it was two years ago, so they did pull down; and with that, they put $18 million into rainy day fund, so the Legislature is tightening its belt in these tougher economic times. He noted out of that, this session, they went in as a County with 12 appropriations requests across a range of spectrum of transportation issues, water issues, and they were able to get six of those funded; two of those did end up getting vetoed in the end; all in all, the County ended up with $6.87 million that was funded from the Legislature; $500,000 of that was vetoed; the two items that were vetoed were the multi-basin study at Miramar Road, Martin Road, and Fisk Boulevard, and then the signal at Caddington Drive and Stadium, which all are very aware of; along with the County’s request, the Sheriff did put a request in this year for $5 million for his Animal Care Center, which they were able to get the full appropriation on that, as some of the Commissioners were at the groundbreaking, he believes it was last week; and then, beyond that, the County, through the transportation work program and the different grants that brought in $281.5 million to the County to fulfill those needs. He pointed out besides that, it was a very slow year with regard to legislation; this year there was 1,896 measures that were filed and only 237 that were passed; 192 of those were general bills, so for those that have been familiar with that process, that is a very slow year; that is a lot of battling back and forth between the House and Senate on coming to terms on agreeing on the different issues; and he thinks the greatest victory of all that the County had is being able to secure the funding that they did based on a budget that is smaller than it was two years ago, and knowing that there are less resources in the different buckets that they create, that can go out to the counties. He mentioned the Governor did end up vetoing just under a billion dollars; of that, as he told the Board, $500,000 of it were issues that the County asked for funding on, and then Commissioner Adkinson has an issue near and dear to her, the Senate Bill (SB) 180 glitch Bill that the Senate passed unanimously, but the House did not take it up; everybody wonders why; there is a lot of internal politics on that; he does know, in speaking with the Senate sponsor, that he is intending to bring that back again next year; and under new leadership, the Board may see a House that is more interested in that issue this time around. He stated with that, again, he would send the Board the information on some of the different bills that may impact the County with regard to growth management, water resources, transportation, and those types of things; and he would be happy to answer any questions.
Chair Altman expressed his appreciation to Mr. Crisafulli for presenting to the Board, and for the hard work he puts in during the legislative session.
Mr. Crisafulli expressed his appreciation to the Board for all of its communication throughout session; he or she is always there to answer a call; he knows several of the Commissioners, which he has talked to several times during session when there questions, especially with the property tax issue on the ballot; he knows Attorney Richardson may have mentioned this, but the Attorney General does have 10 days to either appeal or change that language; they will know in very short order what that is going to look like, and if there is an appeal that does take place and how it is accepted versus the language change; and that is in short order for sure.
Chair Altman asked what happens if they do not agree, if the court rules again that it is improper.
Morris Richardson, County Attorney, replied they start to run out of time to get language through that is approved, but Amendment 3 will be one there; he is sure they will get to a place where it is . . .
Chair Altman interjected by saying will the court write the language.
Attorney Richardson responded he does not believe so.
Sandra Sullivan stated she appreciates Mr. Crisafulli is former House Speaker, has a great deal of knowledge up in Tallahassee and brings a lot of expertise; however, on the Agenda there is an option to go out to Request for Proposals (RFP); she does think that is the appropriate thing to do; she is going to say there are a few conflicts on that recent 222-unit development, he was the lobbyist, she understands, from online for that particular project and also with Health First; it does present a few potentially conflicts of interest; and she also has a bit of heartburn with, what was it, $35,000, she does not know as it has been a while. She went on to say that went to the Political Action Committee (PAC) when Commissioner Feltner was running . . . thanks to Commissioner Feltner for fighting for the Lagoon, stuff; the County tried three times to get him as the County Lobbyist from Ron Book; she just feels that the fair and equitable thing is to go out for RFP, see what comes in, and make an informed decision with everything at hand; he is not negating his abilities, but she would just like to say one thing she came up here and asked about; there are $130 to $197 million costs that the County is looking at putting on ‘we the people’ for the connection by Space Florida; she thinks the Feds and the State need to pay for that; that is a significant amount of money that a promise was made here that that burden would not be put on the ratepayers; yet, the budget indicates it is going to be put on the ratepayers probably after the election; she asked if that is right; and she noted it is not so good optics that really needs to be prioritized for funding so not to put that on them.
Commissioner Pritchett expressed her appreciation to Mr. Crisafulli for all of the work he has done; she stated as far as a lobbyist, she thinks he is hitting it out of the park; she appreciates him having so many connections in the State of Florida; he is nice, so they listen to him, and that is an extra bonus; she expressed her appreciation for Mr. Crisafulli not raising his rates; and she noted there are a lot of pluses to that. She advised she has a quick question; she is sure this is not an issue because she asked the County Attorney about this; there is not a conflict on the things that he is doing other work on as far as the job the County has Mr. Crisafulli doing; and she asked if that is correct, although those guidelines are pretty . . .
Attorney Richardson explained there are two prohibitions in the current Contract; one prohibits SBM from lobbying where the Board of County Commissioners, where there is a conflict of interest; there is another that is just a blanket prohibition against SBM lobbying on behalf of private entities before the Board, regardless of whether there is an actual conflict of interest; that is more of a optics provision than an ethics provision; and if that remains within the Contract, then in his opinion, Mr. Crisafulli, in his capacity as a partner at SBM would not, consistent with the Contract, be able to lobby on behalf of private entities before the Board, so the Board may wish to consider whether to keep that prohibition in or to eliminate it and leave only the prohibition of lobbying when there is an actual conflict of interest.
Commissioner Pritchett asked how long Mr. Crisafulli has lived in Brevard County.
Mr. Crisafulli replied 55 years.
Commissioner Pritchett pointed out he is fighting for his home.
Commissioner Feltner expressed his appreciation to Mr. Crisafulli for all he has done for the County; he stated he thought Mr. Crisafulli would take this moment to tell the Board about what it should anticipate with the implementing language; the referendum was talked about tonight a little bit; maybe while the Commissioners are all here together, he can tell he or she that is going to happen in December; that is going to be during the organizational session; it will be a special session; and he asked what might be anticipated, that process, looking like.
Mr. Crisafulli stated Attorney Richardson actually touched on it; the reality is there is a session of implementation when the language is being put together; they have done this many a time on Statewide initiatives that the Legislature has to come back and work on; the nuance to this one is the State is going to have a new Governor that will have been elected in November, and there is an organizational session that starts November 18th; the likelihood of a special session for implementation, should it pass, would take place likely at that point in time, or during the first committee week that they have now set in the first week of December; the question is does the current governor want the ability to set the standard on what this initiative is going to be while working with the Legislature, because it is important to recognize the Governor does not pass legislation, he just approves it or denies it; and in this case, it is an implementation of a Statewide amendment. He pointed out he does not know the answer to whether or not the Governor gets a final say-so on what the initiative is; he is certainly going to have a foot in the ring when it comes to having this discussion, because this was his initiative to begin with; having said that, the State has two new legislative leaders, Senator Boyd and Speaker Garrison that will be coming in, and they have their own ideas as well; he is certain as they start polling this over the next couple of months, especially with the change in language, that will certainly change the dynamics around the ability for this to pass on the ballot; but as they start polling it, if they start seeing the likelihood that it is going to hit the threshold of 60 percent plus one, they will start formulating their ideas on how they are going to move forward. He commented right now, it is anybody’s guess; he can say this, the Board cannot, but polling always starts higher and finishes lower just because people become more educated, they understand, they hear the impacts it is going to have in their backyard; certainly, there is a conversation to be had on that around the State over the next couple of months; he would be remiss if he did not mention Leader Sirois and Senator Mayfield, in their help this year, helped sponsor each and every one of these budget initiatives and work diligently to get those passed; and he wants to make sure he gives them the proper credit, as well as incoming Senator Boyd who sponsored one of the dredging projects for them just because he likes Brevard County and wanted to see it have some success on that front, so he wanted to make sure he gives a little love to these folks. He reiterated there will be a session, it will be that all will be intimately involved in if in fact there is a conversation that has to take place if a ballot initiative passes.
Commissioner Feltner stated one-quarter of the Legislature changes every other year.
Mr. Crisafulli stated yes, that is correct, there are several people who will not be in that chamber that voted on this; admittedly, a lot of representatives voted on this to give the people a voice, they did not vote on it because they favored or disfavored it, they voted on it to give people a voice on it because it has to go in the Constitution due to the way it is drafted; probably some of them are glad they are not going to be there to implement to be honest; but the truth is, and Commissioner Feltner is right, one-third of that Legislature that put it in place will be there to implement it should they have that opportunity to do so.
Commissioner Feltner mentioned he thinks it is shocking to think one is sworn in, and within a couple of weeks of that, he or she is there for a special session to implement language that could be perhaps the most significant referendum that goes before the voters in quite a long time, so certainly challenges ahead of the Board; for all of those reasons, and for the good work that Mr. Crisafulli has done for the County, he would like to renew the Contract; and that would be his motion today.
Commissioner Adkinson stated she would second the motion.
Attorney Richardson asked if the Board would either address the issue of the prohibition on lobbying activities on behalf of private clients, or perhaps hear from Mr. Crisafulli on that issue.
Mr. Crisafulli stated there is a nuance to it as well; he does not represent SBM Partners when he represents the local clients that he does, he represents them through Crisafulli Consulting; he reiterated that is a nuance, Attorney Richardson is the legal mind, and he does not know how that interacts; he does not represent anyone before the County through SBM Partners; he only represents folks through his Crisafulli Consulting Company; and never in a way that is contrary to the stance that the County has on something, especially on a State issue as it is just not the way to do business. He went on to say he wants to be clear on that nuance, because he does have all of those folks contracted under Crisafulli Consulting.
Attorney Richardson commented he is just looking for the Board’s understanding of that provision and what the Board’s pleasure is with regard to that contractual issue, whether or not the Board is okay with Mr. Crisafulli doing that kind of representation; again, it is not an ethical conflict; that is already addressed by a separate prohibition; it is just a blanket ban on all lobbying on private activities in the Contract; and staff can clarify that, depending on the Board’s direction.
Commissioner Feltner stated he thinks Attorney Richardson said there was a clear conflict earlier, when a clear conflict presents itself.
Attorney Richardson advised just when there is a conflict that prohibition is in there, but that is not going to change; there is a secondary clause that no lobbying whatsoever, conflict or not, on behalf of a private client exists in the current SBM Contract; there are nuances to whether or not that applies to Mr. Crisafulli’s activities; but for staff’s direction moving forward, is the Board’s intention that the consultant and Mr. Crisafulli cannot lobby on behalf of those private interests even when there is no conflict, or would the Board be amenable to modifying the language.
Chair Altman stated it sounds like the Board needs to fix that to disallow lobbying if there is a direct conflict.
Commissioner Adkinson noted yes, she would agree with that.
Attorney Richardson stated staff can make that revision.
Commissioner Adkinson asked if there is a way the Board to structure the motion so it can make that clear.
Attorney Richardson responded if the motion incorporates that, just strike the blanket prohibition on lobbying activities and retain the prohibition on lobbying when there is a conflict of interest; and that will be enough direction.
The Board granted renewal of the Contract with SBM Partners; directed staff to strike the blanket prohibition on lobbying activities and retain the prohibition on lobbying when there is a direct conflict of interest; and authorized the Chair to execute the Contract.

Juanita Jackson, Housing and Human Services Director, explained Item J.2. is a request for a letter of support for the Housing Authority of Brevard County for disposition of Lake View Pointe to Space Coast Community Development Corporation, a Housing Authority’s nonprofit affiliate; Lake View Pointe was constructed in 1964 and consists of 56 public housing units servicing low-income households; the property’s age, deteriorating infrastructure, and functional limitation is affecting the Housing Authority’s ability to provide quality housing efficiently; the Housing Authority development strategy is to transfer ownership of Lake View Pointe to Space Coast Community Development Corporation, request tenant protection vouchers and permission demo from Housing and Urban Development (HUD); once all tenants have been relocated, then demolish Lake View Pointe; Lake View Pointe redevelopment construction would be in late 2029 to mid-2030; future redevelopment will include no fewer than 56 affordable units; and subject to HUD’s approval and final relocation plan, the Housing Authority will provide affected residents with all notices, advisory services, relocation assistance, and moving assistance, and comparable housing opportunities required by HUD.
Richard Heffelfinger commented he does not usually get involved with public housing or any of that stuff, because . . . he will not get into any of that stuff to go into why he does not; this is confusing because he does not understand, it looks like the County is taking something that is funded by Brevard County through housing development dollars that are given, he guesses primarily by the State, and it is running this development, or it owns it; he asked if the County owns it; he noted so, the County owns it, maintains it as low . . . okay, the County does not own it, it manages it; no, it does not manage it; and he asked the County Attorney to keep going as he is learning more as he shakes his head. He stated he really appreciates trying to figure out what is going on because it looks like the housing wants to punt, and they want to punt to a private entity because there is some advantage punting to a private entity; as far as he knows, housing it is a nonprofit when it is kind of public housing; he asked if the County is punting; is it going to get some profit; is the County going to get some profit advantage by knocking it down, building it up; are the same number of units going to be replaced for low-income housing; are the costs going to be higher; and he stated it is going to be better, grant it.
Chair Altman stated to let the Board hear all of the cards, and staff will answer his questions and just who owns who.
Mr. Heffelfinger stated supposedly this outfit, Space Coast Community Development Corporation, is actually part of Housing Authority of Brevard County (HABC) now, yet it is still confusing; it sounds like who owns it now like talking about the water plant; he asked if the special district owns it or . . . so he is wary of that kind of shenanigans like what could possibly be the advantage; he advised somebody is going to get an advantage; and that are his questions.
Sandra Sullivan remarked in 1950 the County formed this entity of HABC; the Housing Authority of Brevard County as a quasi-governmental thing; when one looks up on Sunbiz, there is no such entity; by looking at who is, and she sent an email earlier, when going to Sunbiz, there are all of these businesses here at 1401 Guava Avenue in Melbourne, the location, which are these two of the entity of who the County wants to convey this property to that it says is a wholly-owned nonprofit affiliate, but then when looking up who this guy is, he is associated with a lot of developments, not just in Florida, but outside of Florida; and she is just going to say, this looks stinky. She pointed out it is like HABC does not exist, according to Sunbiz, and yet there are 374 properties that are all in the Housing Authority of Brevard County in the Property Appraisers, and then now the County is going to do something unprecedented; those are going to be put into another entity, but there is nothing to support that it is wholly-owned nonprofit affiliate; she asked the Board to defer this for today until there are additional documents put up; but she will just say, coming to these meetings for eight years, and the stink, she is just not happy with Commissioner Pritchett being back on the Board appointed, given some of the stinky stuff that has gone on that in having to come to these meetings and disclose that; $30 million to Driftwood, and she could make a long list of oh, no, she is looking at the Agenda again and rolling her eyes like not again; and the next four months are going to be hell she thinks, District 1.
Chair Altman advised he is actually looking forward to them.
Jim Liesenfelt, County Manager, stated all staff is asking for, as the subject says on the Agenda, is a letter of support for the Housing Authority of Brevard County; they are not part of the County, they have the name Brevard County, they are not Brevard County; they are the Housing Authority one finds pretty much everywhere across the country; they have their own nonprofit to work on the development; and all they are doing is look for a letter of support from the County.
The Board authorized the Chair to execute a Letter of Support approving HABC’s proposed disposition of Lake View Pointe and transfer ownership to Space Coast Community Development Corporation.
