action_text:
Robert Proffitt commented he is not asking the Board to reopen the site plan, he is asking it to break a deadlock its own staff created; Section 62-2117(c)(4)(a) where BU-1 abuts residential and this lot does commercial vehicles used with that business must sit at the rear and be screened on all four sides by an opaque barrier; on April 10th zoning rejected this plan for that exact reason; seven weeks later with nothing physically changed it was approved; staff now claims C3 governs because these vehicles are only loading; C3 answers whether a truck may be on the property, it says nothing about where it sits or what screens it; C4A answers those questions for lots next to their homes; and if every delivery can be called temporarily, C4A never applies to anyone. He stated what was approved, east and south rely on an existing masonry wall; no height, no ownership, and no permit in the file; west is the building, north is the landscape buffer that was reduced not made opaque; under the Code’s own definition, two sides are unproven and two sides are not barrier; that is not a four-sided screening; the site plan calls this a vintage car showroom; the sealed drawings differ; unconditional low bay, almost no glass, five rollup doors facing the houses, a parts mezzanine, and ventilation that works only if those doors stay open; the operator advertises more than 100 vehicles in an inventory; and a showroom is not ventilated by leaving the garage doors open. He noted the County Attorney’s letter agrees on the next step; if the use is parking, staging, or storage, not unloading, the four-sided screen applies; nothing on the approved plan stops the inventory from sitting on the east stalls on the residential side once off the trailer, that is the deadlock; direct the County Attorney and the building official to issue one written dated determination before the permit is released, which subsection applies, where on the plan a commercial vehicle may sit, and the ownership height and permit status of the wall, one answer on the record; that writing must also address occupancy and fire area, and prohibit staging in the east stalls; the Code was written to protect the homes next door; and he asked the Board to direct staff to put in writing that it is being followed before any Certificate of Occupancy (CO) issues.
Carol Frick remarked she is appearing before the Board tonight because she is concerned about the sidewalk to nowhere; it is being mandated along the east side of U.S. 1 along the new Rokku Tana automobile dealership; it is her understanding that the installation of sidewalks on a new commercial development is mandatory on residential resale, or residential sale, or construction; there is no mandate for sidewalks; she understands it is Brevard County’s wish and/or objective to have sidewalks along the entire length of U.S. 1; however, at this point, the Rokku Tana development will be the only property with sidewalks for miles; and they go from nowhere to nowhere. She pointed out there are no other commercial lots south of Helmsman Place, past South Indian River Isles development to where the County owns a small parcel across from Landscape Depot, nor are there commercial properties to the north end of Helmsman Place, past the Indian River Isles North development, all the way up until she thinks it is called Ruente Place, which she believes is an access road back to a meter pit; due to the installation of the sidewalks to nowhere, Indian River Isles South will be forced to remove their community sign on the south side of their entrance; the north sign will remain; however, it is not going to be visible going south on U.S. 1 at all to be honest; while the installation of sidewalks along U.S. 1 is a dream, with only residential properties along the contiguous properties along U.S. 1 and no sidewalks are required on residential resale or development, the likelihood of continuous sidewalks seems extremely unlikely way into the future. She stated unless the County could be the recipient of a Federal grant for sidewalk installation, or somehow or the other the County Commissioners find tens of thousands of unappropriated dollars for sidewalk installation, it is not going to happen, it just is not, it is a pipe dream; everybody would probably love to see it, but it is not going to happen; tonight they are asking the Board to reconsider its ruling that sidewalks are necessary at the Rokku Tana dealership and grant a waiver recurrent of removing the condition allowing Indian River Isles to keep their community sign monument; and she expressed her appreciation to the Board for its time and the re-evaluation of the mandatory report.
Bonnie Walls stated they understand that this property is commercially zoned; they understand that the owner has a right to develop the property, but tonight she is asking the Board to consider something that goes beyond a zoning designation on a map; she is asking the Board to consider what this particular development will do to the entrance and character of an established residential community; every home in Indian River Isles is either brick or stucco, that was not an accident; over the years, the community has developed a beautiful, cohesive, architectural character; and it is part of that that makes this place special and part of what attracted many of them to live there. She continued by saying the entrance of their community they will soon have a large, metal warehouse-type building take shape; once that building is finished, it will be there for decades; she asked is a large, exposed, metal building really the best transition between the commercial corridor on U.S. 1 and the residential community behind it; she mentioned they are not asking for a residential building, they are not asking that commercial development be prohibited, they are asking for good design; they are asking that the developer recognize that this not an isolated, commercial parcel somewhere in the middle of nowhere, it is effectively the gateway to their neighborhood; the portion of this building that faces their community should look like it was thoughtfully designed out for its location, not like the backside of a warehouse that could have been built anywhere; and they believe the building should incorporate architectural materials such as brick, stucco, masonry, or comparable, high quality materials. She stated they also understand that the road is public; public does not mean that the impact on the surrounding residential community should be ignored; they are asking the County to look at the whole picture, look at the location, look at the surrounding homes, look at the entrance of their community, look at the permanent visual impact this building will have, and ask whether or not there is a better way to develop this property while still respecting the rights of all of the property owners at Indian River Isles, because once that metal building is finished, they cannot move it; the architectural character cannot easily be changed and their community will live with that every single day; she respectfully asked the County and the developer to do better; she noted do not simply build what is technically permissible; build something that is appropriate for this location and their neighborhood; give them a building that respects the community next door, give them meaningful landscaping and screening, give them architectural materials that complement the brick and stucco homes that surround it, and give them a development that can coexist with Indian River Isles rather than becoming a permanent eyesore at its front door, and they are not asking for special treatment, they are asking for thoughtful development, responsible design, and respect for the community that they all will have to live in long after everyone in this room has gone home.
Jeffrey Lee commented he has been a 42-year resident of Brevard and has lived in the current address for 13 years; the Board has heard some pretty interesting things; he is bringing up in a pretty different topic on the subject of safety; while they know there is a commercial lot at the front of their neighborhood, they know they live on public streets; what none of them here ever thought there would be is a car dealership and driving through the neighborhood on a routine basis; and he asked what the basis is of that statement. He advised number one, the dealership specifies in Japanese market cars, JMDs as they are called, and mini trucks; mini trucks are defined by Florida Statute as vehicles that generally are not supposed to go over 55 miles an hour and are restricted from any road with a speed limit greater than 35 miles an hour; in order to even operate the vehicle, they can only drive in their neighborhood; they are not legally allowed to drive on U.S. 1 at all; their asks are pretty straightforward; the neighborhood, as people mentioned, they do not have sidewalks; everybody walks, jogs, and rides bikes with their kids in the neighborhood; and there is no other way but being in the street. He pointed out this residential speed limit of 20 miles an hour, while it could be enforced, the roads do not go anywhere, so all they can do is drive up and down the cul-de-sacs and back and forth; their primary concern is safety; this is about all of the people here; they have multiple families with special needs household members that need to be considered; they have looked at a few of the statutes to look at what could at least be proposed as some ideas; one, clearly the mini truck rules can be extended; there could be a safety concern in the neighborhood to prohibit the driving of these vehicles, because they are also insured under the dealership; and they are really not registered and titled directly by the owners who own them. He stated they would like to see if the Board could consider establishing an objective that test drives are not conducted in the neighborhood; he does not know how the County could allow them to test drive vehicles without driving them around in the neighborhood; the cars do not fall under this rule; they can go out on U.S. 1, so that would be what they would hope the Board would do; but nothing prevents them from driving around the neighborhood; the Board can also exercise authority under Florida Statute 316.2122 and specifically prohibit the operation of mini trucks in their neighborhood; that is something that from his reading is it would be empowered to do; they do not want to undo the commercial development that is taking place, but the safety, to the best of his knowledge, there have been no traffic studies; there has been no impact studies and vehicular traffic in a truly closed neighborhood; the roads, just like the sidewalks that are not there and do not go anywhere; and their streets do not have anything either.
Mark Minor stated he believes he is the longest tenured resident of South Indian River Isles; he purchased his property from the Altman family in 1988, and built his home where he raised his family; for nearly 40 years, it has been his, his family’s home, not simply an investment; tonight the Board is going to hear, or have already heard, about zoning, building Codes, permits, Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT), and other technical issues surrounding the proposed used car facility to be located at Helmsman Place; and those issues matter and they deserve serious answers. He asked the Board to look beyond the paperwork tonight, and to look at the people and the families; he mentioned more than 70 families live in this neighborhood; they have all paid their property taxes, school taxes, fire assessments, and supported this community for decades; they have invested their money, their families, and their lives here with each other; and now they are being asked to accept a large, commercial operation to be located essentially feet from their homes, an operation that will fundamentally and permanently change the character, safety, and quality of lives of their entire neighborhood community. He stated to believe him, the only difference between the Commissioners sitting up there and he standing here is happenstance; he asked if this were his or her home or family, and neighborhood, how would he or she feel and react; he pointed out, indeed, it could very well be he or she standing here someday addressing the Commission; the Altman family sale of this property is not a personal criticism of Commissioner Altman or his family, quite to the contrary, he highly respects Commissioner Altman and his many years of distinguished public service as a Senator, Congressman, and now Commissioner, and considers him a friend, but all of the Commissioners have a responsibility and an obligation to protect the best interest of the Brevard County residents that it represents, not simply just to determine whether a project can technically meet minimum requirements that were probably written decades ago by people who are not even alive today; and the minimum standards do not always equal common sense. He stated accommodating this business means changing or destroying their neighborhood entrance signs, removing their entrance safety meeting median, or creating sidewalks to nowhere and bringing commercial traffic into an established residential community; he asked the Board to step back, take a look at the bigger picture; does this really make sense; he stated the business developer can build and move on; and he asked if they do, who will then take their place. He noted the neighborhood will have to live with the consequences of these decisions, he or she does not; he is not against growth or new business, but growth should not come at the irreversible expense of families who have spent decades building their lives in this neighborhood; and he respectfully asked the Board to put his or herself in their shoes, listen to its residents for once, and do not confuse governmental rules written long ago with just plain old-fashioned common sense.
Jim Harvey advised he is here today because he is concerned about Rokku Tana automobile dealership conducting vehicle test drives through their neighborhood; their subdivision is home to 72 families, 14 of those families have children under the age of 15, and two children with special needs; he understands the dealership needs to conduct test drives; he also understands that customers need an opportunity to evaluate a vehicle before a major purchase; his concern is not with the test drives themselves, his concern is where those test drives are taking place and the impact they will have on their residential neighborhood; their neighborhood was designed and intended only for residents, families, children, pedestrians, cyclists, and normal residential traffic; and it was not intended to function as a test drive automobile route for automobile dealerships. He continued by saying a test drive is different from ordinary residential driving; a potential buyer may be evaluating acceleration, braking, handling, turning, or other vehicle characteristics; they have people walking, children playing, residents backing out of driveways, homeowners walking their pets, and cycles sharing these same roads; they should have to wonder whether the vehicle coming around the corner is simply someone’s daily commute or a dealership customer testing how quickly the car accelerates or how it handles; he asked the Commission if it could consider whether dealerships should be required or encouraged to conduct test drives on roads like U.S. 1 that are better suited; and Rokku’s development has created numerous challenges for the 72 families in this once quiet neighborhood. He respectfully asked the Commission to investigate the issue and approve the recommendations Jeff Lee previously; and he expressed his appreciation to the Board for listening to his concerns.
Patricia Chaffiot stated she has been a Brevard County resident for 25 years, and she has lived at 6215 Capstan Court for the past 18 years; she is presenting to the Board a question that has arisen in their neighborhood; the property at 651 Helmsman Place is zoned BU-1; she asked why it is not zoned BU-1-A; she advised this designation, per the County Code, is for commercial lots that abut commercial property, which is clearly the case here; it is by definition a restricted neighborhood retail commercial zoning classification that encompasses land devoted to limited retail, shopping, and personal services to serve the needs of low density residential neighborhoods; and if this zoning had been assigned to this property, then there is no way this project would have been approved in their neighborhood. She went on to say there are a list of business types allowed under BU-1-A and the type of businesses are very limited; this is the whole purpose of this zoning classification to protect residential neighborhoods; and she asked again why the commercial property is not zoned BU-1-A.
Chair Altman stated the next speaker is Debbie Goode.
Someone from the audience noted Ms. Goode was on her way, she had another meeting, she has left, but she has another five minutes before she gets here.
Chair Altman stated the Board might be able to still be here; it has Board Reports; he reiterated that is the last speaker; and he asked why not open it up for questions from the Board.
Commissioner Feltner asked what the dealership has done that is conveyed that they are going to test drive cars in the nearby neighborhood, and is that something they stated, or how did that come to be.
Ms. Gilliam replied she thinks that is just an assumption of the residents; there is nothing on the site plan to indicate their test drive routes; and they have not said anything to staff about using the neighborhood for that.
Commissioner Feltner stated he understands these are JDM cars, Japanese Domestic car; he is the resident car guy on the Commission; he thinks they understand they want to import K cars; the K cars have an exemption after 25 years; it says they do not have to meet emissions and other safety equipment; they can be driven on every road in Florida; there is no prohibition for them even to take them on the highway; it is not something he would do; he has seen some of those, one sees them out there, but they are more than 25 years old; and when one sees them at a gas station or on the road . . . and he thinks a big part of buying one of those cars is that someone has imported, because that is what has happened. He continued by saying they became popular to import once they are past the 25 years; one absolutely would want to take them and drive them on U.S. 1 because he would not want to buy something that he could not handle on a road in Brevard County; and he does not even know how one gets a car to an area where he or she is only going to drive at 35 miles per hour and never have to cross another road that would be 50 miles per hour, so he does not know why one would want to drive it in a neighborhood as opposed to U.S.1. He noted something that occurred to him, and he thinks this is a technical question for staff, he is just talking in theory and talking out loud here for a second, and he asked if it is possible for South Indian River Isles to become a private road; he stated he knows the County is further along, but it has this conversation around here quite a lot these days; he has something in his District that is not . . . it is different; but there is a similar conversation being had at this point in their existence; and he asked if that option is available to them.
Ms. Gilliam replied yes, Commissioner, some of the residents actually met with Public Works last week, with Lauren Holman, and she discussed that with them; they also discussed maybe putting up a gate as well; and they have all of the information, and the packet that they need the application and to move forward with that.
Commissioner Feltner asked if by virtue of it being a private road, they could put up a gate and that would control everyone going in and out of their neighborhood.
Ms. Gilliam responded affirmatively.
Commissioner Feltner asked if that potentially would not have an immediate cost to them, and obviously, they would own the road and would own the sidewalks, or is there, he does not know.
Mr. Prasad explained there could be a cost because in order to meet the Code requirements, they perhaps would have to put in a turnaround; when people do turn off for the U.S. 1 and if they could not go to the gate, so there could be a cost of . . .
Commissioner Feltner interjected by saying so in front of their neighborhood, one would have to be able to get back out of there, okay, that seems like that might be a tradeoff there; as far as the zoning, that was an interesting question; he does not know how they originally ended up with BU-1, but he is sure that is a legacy thing; the County cannot do an adverse zoning change at this point without the owner coming in and seeking that change, it would not just be able to impose that on; and he asked if that is fair.
Ms. Gilliam replied yes, the original zoning is from 1973 actually.
Morris Richardson, County Attorney, pointed out the Board could impose that on them, but the County would have to pay for that.
Commissioner Feltner noted he understands; it seems like there are a couple of options moving forward, so he thinks this will come to the Board; and as far as the sidewalk and the sign issue, he does not think it is 100 percent settled on that today.

Stephanie Palacios, Director of Advocacy and Government Relations for Second Harvest Food Bank of Central Florida, stated they have the pleasure of serving this community as well as seven total counties in Central Florida; they cannot do the work they do without the partner agency network; they have 84 partner agencies in Brevard County that are doing this work every day; they are working with neighbors, working with them, and serving families, children, and seniors in the community; one thing she can ask and she thanks the Board for allowing her to ask, is for the community to volunteer; Hunger Action Month is a time where people can take action and the action that people can take is to work at a non-profit near oneself, that is close to their own heart; many of their partner agencies ask them to help recruit volunteers because that is something that they struggle to do; and so she will call to the community if there is a church or pantry nearby, that someone was wanting to help, now is the time to volunteer. She went on to say their branch in Melbourne can accept volunteers as well, about 25; if anyone has not been to the branch in Melbourne, please feel free to reach out to her, she would be happy to give someone a tour and share a little about what they do; that is a call to the community; anyone who wants to come visit for a tour, please come, they would love to have them; and she expressed her appreciation to the Board, commenting it is nice to see all of them.
Chair Altman expressed his appreciation to her for what she does; he commented they have 11 counties; and he asked if she lives in Melbourne.
Ms. Palacios advised it is seven counties, and that she lives in Seminole County, which happens to be right in the middle of all seven.

action_text:
Tracy Duda Chapman, Duda Chief Legal and Administrative Officer, expressed her appreciation to the Board on behalf of the Duda family and the company; she stated this is a major milestone and they have been celebrating with a tagline of Duda, 100 years strong, because they really are blessed to have really amazing employees, past and present, who have really made the company what it is today; and they have honored those employees throughout the celebration. She mentioned as was said, Viera is named Faith, and the company really is driven by faith in terms of the decisions that it makes; she would say she thinks the three seniors, her grandfather and his two brothers, as they rode horses, looking at the Brevard County Cocoa Ranch when they first purchased it in the 50’s and 60’s, that they had faith that one day it could be something else; the third generation really had faith when they decided to embark on a real estate business in 1989; she just wanted to say thanks to Brevard County for having faith in the company that it could develop a community that people would want to live in right here in Central Brevard County; and she thinks the company has delivered on that promise. She also expressed her appreciation to the County, staff, the Commission, and past Commissions and staff because they all made a difference in the success.
Todd Pokrywa, Duda Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of the Real Estate Group, stated he would like to add a couple of things to what Ms. Chapman just shared; he has the great privilege of working for Duda, and leading the real estate group here in Brevard County; they have hundreds of employees across all of its business operations here locally, and many more that had preceded them; on behalf of all of them he would thank the Board; they have a great partnership with the County; they would not be able to do what they have done and be ranked as one of the top selling master plan communities in the country, without that collaboration that they have with the Board, Brevard County government, as well as all the other major stake holders here on the space coast; he mentioned they have 16,000 homes that have been developed to date, four million square feet of office and commercial space, over 1,000 jobs in the mast plan community of Viera, and there is still a long runway in front of them, so they are expanding the tax base, creating value, and providing a place for people to live, work, and play; and he expressed appreciation to the Board once again, for the recognition of the 100th anniversary.
Commissioner Feltner advised it is an honor for him to be the Viera and Suntree Commissioner; he is always excited about the new things that open up, and he considers himself as an ambassador; anyone who comes to meet with him, he asks if he or she has been to the new Olive Tree, it is beautiful this time of year, and he does a lot of that enjoying all the new things that are brought to Viera; and it is an exciting place to be.

action_text:
Johnette Gindling, President and CEO of the Space Coast Health Foundation, stated the Board’s action today is important because Brevard County is the only one of Florida’s 67 counties where all municipalities and governing bodies pass proclamations and resolutions to support efforts to prevent suicide; it is another reason why this County is special; on the space coast, the suicide numbers hit a little harder because Brevard has one of the highest suicide rates in Florida; more than 17 people annually for every 100,000 people; they do not know why it is higher in Brevard, but the Space Coast Health Foundation and its partners are committed to reversing it; and if there is one thing that people can do individually, maybe it is just being there for someone who is physically distressed. She went on to say in 2000 a young man named Kevin Hines jumped off the Golden Gate Bridge in San Francisco; he somehow survived and is now leading advocacy work for suicide prevention and mental health; prior to jumping, Kevin said he was walking on the bridge, sobbing and clearly in poor emotional state; no one asked him what was wrong; Kevin said if someone would have stopped him and asked if he was okay, he probably would not have jumped; people, take that lesson and always be that person who asks if everything is okay, to someone who is in need; it is likely to make a difference in someone’s life; and she expressed her appreciation for the Board’s support.
Kelly Haskins, Founder of Do it For Hunter, stated Do it for Hunter is a local nonprofit based out of Merritt Island; it has been around since they lost Hunter almost five years ago; it will be five years the end of this month; they do may activities in the community to bring the “you matter” message to the community; she knows everyone has heard those words, but they are more of a boots on the ground type and they do things to try to make a difference; herself and Colleen both lost their kids and this is what they do; they do have an event coming up this Saturday, called You Matter Day; it will be the fifth annual and it started as a lemonade stand and now it has progressed to a really great community event; and she hopes the Board can come, it is located at Merritt Island High School, from 9:00 am until 1:00 pm.
Chair Altman asked Ms. Haskins to share a little bit about Hunter.
Ms. Haskins stated Hunter is her son; he was 18 when they lost him to suicide; they had sent him off to University of Central Florida (UCF) and he had a bad day; that was it; and Emily, the same.
An audience member stated to give a reason, Emily was 18 years old, she went to Florida State University (FSU) and took her life; it should not be happening and they want to make awareness.
Ms. Haskins commented one is too many and the goal is to save just one.
Kristen Wary, representing 2-1-1 Brevard, expressed her appreciation for the Board’s support; she stated as the Board knows 2-1-1 Brevard hosts the 9-8-8 Lifeline Crisis call center; it is a very important number for texting and calling; this is their fourth year; to share a few stats from the community dashboard, of the nearly 43,000 contacts, points of contact last year, there were about 5,400 specific to 9-8-8 and the 2-1-1 number as well, that refers to mental health and suicide prevention; that is averaging 400 per month points of contact, whether they come from 9-8-8 or 2-1-1, that relates specifically to suicide and crisis prevention, mental health support; and with their partners this is obviously a very important recognition.
body: Brevard County Board of County Commissioners
title: Resolution recognizing September 2026 as National Suicide Prevention Month - District 5

action_text: Nicole Grabner, Director of One Voice of Brevard, stated she is a disabled veteran and a mother of two children on the spectrum; shew ants to thank the Board for presenting this Resolution proclaiming disability voting rights awareness week in Brevard County; recognizing tis week is far more than a symbolic gesture, it signals to thousands of residents across the County that their voices, their civic contributions, and their fundamental right to participate in local self-governance matters; the ballot box is where the community shapes it future; when voters with disabilities cast their ballots, they are advocating for their essential resources that make daily life possible; accessible infrastructure, strong support systems, and equal opportunity to live independently; the civic participation is especially vital today, as broader discussions around civil rights, regulations evolve, and people are reminded of just how critical it is to protect the core principal of community integration: and the simple truth is that every resident has a right to live, work, and fully participate in their home community. She continued by saying real accessibility does not happen in abstract policies, it happens right here at home through accessible polling places, reliable transportation, and local spaces that keeps all residents integrated and engaged; by issuing this Resolution today, Brevard County is demonstrating that full community access is a priority for all of its residents; voting rights and daily community access goes hand in hand, one cannot have one without the other; She expressed her appreciation for the Board’s leadership, recognizing disability rights awareness week, and for standing with all disabled residents across Brevard County.
attachments: Disability Voting Rights Awareness Week Resolution.pdf

title: Resolution, Re: Disability Voting Rights Awareness Week - District 3

action_text:
Edward Fontanin, Utility Services Director, stated to explain the circumstance, the Sykes Creek wastewater plant, the dewatering equipment for the biosolids broke and without that equipment there is no way of disposing it; the landfill will not accept it because of the high moisture content; when that occurs that is an emergency situation for them; they issue a $50,000 emergency Purchase Order (PO) which allows the vendor to proceed; and it is a mechanism to start the project with the understanding that upon the completion of the work, staff comes back to the Board to reconcile the remaining amount, which is what the $340,000 is. He went on to say the equipment is soon to be repaired and should be concluded by the end of this month; and that is why the Agenda refers to the month of August and September as being the conclusion of this emergency PO.
Richard Heffelfinger inquired if that was competitively bid for the repair.
Chair Altman advised this is not a question and answer, the Board heard his presentation and then staff’s response; but Mr. Fontanin can answer that question; and he reminded Mr. Heffelfinger to get all his questions together in his presentation.
Mr. Fontanin responded because the situation is an emergency, staff did not have time to go out and procure it through an advertisement; in a sense it is defined as an emergency because without this immediate assistance, it would be a violation with the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) which would lead to a consent order; Synagro is quite honestly the only rental company that has such equipment; and this is in the world of utilities in Florida, when situations like this occur, it is 99 percent of the time Synagro who is providing that equipment.
Chair Altman stated he is sure it was competitively quoted and selected, it was not like the County was held at total mercy to the vendor.
Mr. Fontanin replied yes, when there is a reference to an existing contract to use as a basis for the compensation, staff uses that mode.
Jim Liesenfelt, County Manager, stated this also shows the checks and balances; Mr. Fontanin has authority up to 50,000; that is why it is an emergency PO and why it was issued in that amount; the County Manager has the authority of up to $200,000; as seen in the Agenda he signed up to $190,000, and the total cost is $340,000, therefore, it was brought to the Board; and the Board can see this is within the purchasing system and that is how it works.
body: Brevard County Board of County Commissioners
title: Approval, Re: Request for Emergency Purchase Order Payment to Synagro South, LLC for Emergency Mobilization and Dewatering Equipment at Sykes Creek Wastewater Treatment Facility

Chair Altman advised the Board is back on Item J.2.
Commissioner Feltner noted he will say it again, he will go with Commissioner Pritchett on the lifeguards and fund them 100 percent this year; the Board can get that done; he would like to leave the rest in capital at least, and the Board can come back at any time to discuss that; he thinks definitely there could be further discussion there; and item D he is with Commissioner Pritchett on that as well. His motion would be the marketing plan that is in there, fund the full amount the full amount for the lifeguards, and change to authorize that the County Manager be able to access disaster funds, fund 1444, in the event of a state and local emergency; the County Manager shall notify the Board of County Commissioners of all changes at the first Board meeting.
Commissioner Pritchett noted there is not enough in that to totally do lifeguards, part of it will have to be tapped from the Capital Fund.
Commissioner Feltner advised that he agrees with; he thinks he said that; they will take it from Capital because that is one of the things that will be done to spend down; take that out of capital and he thinks technically it will have to transferred to marketing before it is spent on lifeguards.
Mr. Cranis replied that is how it works; it is $889,949 and it would leave a remaining amount of $1.8 million in the Capital Fund.
Commissioner Feltner stated he will include that into his motion, the transfer.
Commissioner Pritchett mentioned to Commissioner Feltner that item C., when staff does the spending, it does have to have it reported on a quarterly thing, and that is what item C. is; that is happening with what was wanted in that, but after the spending, the Board receives a quarterly report of all the spending that was done for those things, as the Board of County Commissioners.
Commissioner Feltner stated he does not have a problem with item C.
Commissioner Pritchett pointed out this request is actually good for you other than coming back with how to do the Capital Funds, and she asked if he wanted to do that later.
Commissioner Feltner responded affirmatively, stating that he wants to leave the rest, but to take out the $889,000 from Capital and move it to Marketing, then pay 100 percent of the lifeguards; that is going to free up $889,000 for General Fund.
Commissioner Pritchett stated that was kind of what she was looking for and the Board can talk about capital later if it has to do something.
Commissioner Feltner stated he will include Item C. for the quarterly reporting and then Item D, what he read earlier about the County Manager being able to access disaster funds.
Commissioner Pritchett noted that way the Board itself can maybe come up with ideas, if it has any ideas for the capital expenses of what can be done to help increase tourism, but still alleviate some pressure off the General Fund next year.
Chair Altman advised he has a number of questions and he wants to make sure the Board completely understands what is being done here; and he inquired where money is being taken from because he wants to specifically know what is being cut.
Commissioner Feltner stated from the Capital Fund, the County will take $889,000; and he inquired with Mr. Cranis if there are any Capital obligations for that money that is sitting, so far.
Mr. Cranis advised that the $2.7 million is unallocated and not committed to anything; and the number is $889,949 for the lifeguards.
Commissioner Feltner commented as a Tourism Council they were trying to build that fund back up because it was a t about $900,000 or a little bit below; from the Capital take $889,949 and transfer it to marketing then immediately take it from marketing to pay for the last quarter of the lifeguard program; and that will free up that $189,000 for General Fund for the County.
Chair Altman asked how much that will leave for Capital.
Mr. Cranis replied $1.8 million would be remaining in Capital.
Chair Altman commented and those projects have not been selected yet.
Mr. Cranis replied no, those would be free and clear dollars for now.
Chair Altman thanked Commissioner Feltner for clarifying that, and he called the question.
The Board approved the proposed FY 2026-2027 Marketing and Media Plan for the TDO in the total amount of $15,027,500, including the selection of the media vendors listed in the 2026-2027 Marketing Plan presentation; approved you to negotiate and execute contracts, contract amendments, and any necessary contracts for selected marketing, media, and advertising firms within the Board approved FY 2026-2027 Marketing and Media Plan, upon review and approval by the County Attorney’s Office, Risk Management, and Purchasing Services, in accordance with Administrative Order AO-29, “Contract and Grant Administration,” up to and exceeding $200,000, the total amount not to exceed $15,027,500 without additional Board approval, and an additional caveat that the TDO send a quarterly report to the Board on spending by contract, vendor, and amount, with Commission approval for material changes to the Marketing Plan; authorized the County Manager be able to access Disaster Funds (Fund 1444) in the event of a State or local emergency declaration, natural or man-made disaster for the purposes of advertising/marketing/promotional costs of up to and exceeding $200,000, the total amount not to exceed $1,548,712, with the County Manager notifying the Board of all changes at the first Board meeting; and authorized an additional $889,949 be moved from the Capital Fund to the Marketing Fund and directed to the lifeguard program.

action_text:
Richard Heffelfinger stated he is going to use his public comment to once again appeal to the Board about the $5 million for an animal shelter that the Sheriff asked for that the Board was going to provide the $5 million by busting the cap for an animal shelter; if the Board looks at the Charter it says, “notwithstanding paragraphs A and B, the Board of County Commissioners may impose an ad valorem tax for County, municipal, or district purposes at a rate which exceeds limitation in paragraph A and B. If a supermajority of the Board, “which the Board had, “concurs in a finding that such an excess is necessary because of emergency or critical need”; he could read the Board the definition of an emergency, a condition of urgent need for action or assistance, a serious situation, or occurrence that happens unexpectedly and demand immediate attention, an unforeseen occurrence, and that is just a few; what about critical needs, a sudden occurrence, a critical need can emerge, emergency situation, pressing necessity; he commented he does not think it meets any of those; as a matter of fact during the budget workshops it was not mentioned until the third workshop; it managed to show up as an unfunded need; it is an animal shelter and he does not see where it is public safety, that is referred to in some of the write up to justify it in the Resolution that the Board presented back on September 8; it does not meet those requirements; it is a violation of the County Charter; and that $5 million needs to come off of there. He went on to say the Board could have put that $5 million somewhere else and he would not have said anything because the Board had a whole list of critical needs and emergencies; if it wants to talk about a real public safety emergency it is that six-story building; they have sewage running down in the building, that is bad; it is putting those people at risk and yet the Board is designating $5 million, the largest designation according to the reason for busting the cap; he would also question the numbers on the millage that the Board increased and the amount of money that it is going to yield; it is asking for $902,580 more than what was allocated in the critical need; he does not know where that money goes; to do the math on the sheets, it is asking for more than it needs and asking for $5 million that does not meet the charter requirement; and he does not know what action it would take for the Board to have to go further to justify that. He mentioned the Sheriff says it is critical, but he does not see it, and he does not think anyone can see it; he just wanted to come up here, this Board talks about hunger and it is spending $5 million that is causing taxes to go up on people that are pushing their ability to pay right now; and people have insurance, and now the Board is busting the cap and raising their real estate tax.
Chair Altman stated he would like to say something on that since the Board took a vote on something that was critical; he thinks anyone who actually has been in that shelter and saw the dire straits, it is a very old facility and it has been there for quite some time, it is an emergency situation; animal control is core to the Board’s mission; it is a public health issue; and he believes this Board was justified and he wanted to say that for the record.
Jennifer Mark stated she would like to ask the Board for consideration in discussing the puppies store at 1714 Riverside Drive in Titusville; she drives by this store a few times per week and every time her heart hurts; she sees the same cars in the parking lot and she never sees dogs in the yard; she emailed this store to ask what this puppies business was and she received no response; from their website, people can tell what this business is, they are selling dogs; some of the photos look like these puppies have grown into dogs and have lived their puppy year in a cage; in 2021 Orange County Commissioners enacted an ordinance to shut down the puppy mill pipeline into that county; and they joined 70 other jurisdictions to ban this activity within the great state of Florida. She went on to say at this time the owner of this store just skipped on down 50 into Titusville and set up shop in Brevard County on riverfront property; this puppy store, named in the tax records, is Breeders Pick Orlando, Inc. and it brings in a whopping $160 to Titusville; the owner has registered his puppy selling store as retail sales, so these dogs are considered retail, like a shoe; she has dogs that wait in the window every day much like many others have; one of her dogs gets extreme anxiety during thunderstorms; and she thinks of these poor pups in this store living in these cages who are scared and alone every night. She commented looking at their website and these pictures will make someone sick; to no surprise there are no comments of this business on the Better Business Bureau; however, there is a big red alert on the profile; the AKC and the BBB offer advice to the consumers to do their research of where these dogs come from; on August 14, she called the Brevard County Animal Services line and she also sent an email to Sheriff Wayne Ivey; she received a call back from Jennifer Strait, animal services supervisor, who was directed by Sheriff Ivey to do an investigation; she is still waiting on that report; and Ms. Strait suggested she take this up at the Titusville meeting, which she did, and her she is today. She noted Mayor Connors at the Titusville meeting said they are going to discuss this matter at their meeting in private; on another note, back in 2019, Brevard County Commissioner Bryan Lober initially proposed a strict adoption model which would allow rescued and shelter dogs be sold in pet stores only; currently, there is a pet store in the Melbourne Mall and these puppies are not rescues or strays; it sounds antiquated to her that there is still a business selling dogs in a mall; they are in cages with wire floors and it is cruel; and she is asking for assistance in next steps to get these puppy mill pipeline stores banned in Brevard County, like the neighboring Orange County.
Chair Altman expressed his appreciation for bringing this to the Board’s attention.

Chair Altman called for a public hearing to adopt a resolution listing the inventory of all real property within the County’s jurisdiction that is appropriate for use as affordable housing.
Kathy Wall stated in 2023 the Florida legislators changed or updated the Florida Statutes to require counties every three years to post any surplus property that is suitable for affordable housing; the County posted in 2023 and again posting it in 2026, after the Board has a public hearing on the Resolution; the Housing and Human Services Department did a review of the surplus properties and they are recommending taking off seven of those properties; and Juanita Jackson, Housing and Human Services Director is there to explain.
Ms. Jackson stated the properties that staff recommends removing lack adequate improved roadway access and necessary utility infrastructure to support residential development and would require substantial infrastructure improvement beyond those typical of residential site development, therefore making them not affordable; and that is why staff is recommending removal.
Ms. Wall asked the Board to have a public hearing on the attached resolution to accept public comment.
Richard Heffelfinger stated he only has one question; he asked if the County, because those properties are all County-owned, if it will sell those properties to some outfit to then build housing; is that how it works, so there is potential revenue for the County when somebody buys them; or does the County donate them.
Commissioner Feltner asked if it is specifically on the seven that are not suitable because those will be offered to nearby neighbors.
Ms. Wall advised that is correct.
The Board conducted a public hearing and adopted Resolution No. 26-089, that includes an inventory list of all real property within the County’s jurisdiction to which the County holds fee simple title, and which has been found to be appropriate for use as affordable housing.

body: Brevard County Board of County Commissioners
title: Approval, Re: Tourist Development Council (TDC) FY 2026-2027 Marketing Support Program recommendations

action_text:
Peter Cranis, Tourist Development Office Director, stated this is the Tourist Development Office Annual Marketing Plan for the Fiscal Year 2026-2027; it is a plan that is quite comprehensive; it had a lot of public input; it took about six months to put it together; the total budget is $15,027,500; of that $3,069,546 is going to pay for lifeguards and also the grant fund that was just voted on; that leaves a net of $11,957,954 for the marketing and promotions piece of that program; and attached was a marketing plan that both the marketing committee and the Tourist Development Council (TDC) approved unanimously.
Eric Garvey, President of the Cocoa Beach Area Hotel and Lodging Association, stated he is representing 21 members who employ about 4,000 Brevard County residents; the ask is fairly simple, he would ask that the Board approve the marketing plan as presented in the packet; he wants to talk a little bit about how they got there with this plan; over the last couple years, Commissioner Feltner has chaired the TDC and done a great job; he is very appreciative of him, Mr. Cranis, and his team really creating what he thinks could be a model for how a local County works with their hospitality community; and they are collaborating in great spirit, and no longer arguing, which is quite an accomplishment in Brevard County. He went on to say the association is community oriented; a lot of the hotels are owned and operated by locals; he understands the pressure that is on this County and on the local cities as it looks at Amendment 3; people themselves will feel that burden; he expects large increases in the commercial property taxes which affects the operating budgets; with regard to lifeguards, the association supports 100 percent funding the lifeguard program with Tourist Development Tax (TDT); the association just asks that the County do it the right way; and Commissioner Feltner working with representative Tyler Sirois, last year got clear language put into the State Statute so that can be enacted through ordinance and the County can stop pulling that money from other funds that were not intended for; but until that it done, the association fully supports funding lifeguards with TDT. He reiterated the ask is simple; he noted there are over 2,000 hotel units in development right now that will come online in 2017 and 2018; the current annual growth last year was 3.5 percent; this year he thinks it will be somewhere around five or six percent; they will have to keep up that pace to fill the 17; they have to fill up those hotel rooms; and that is the challenge and this plan addresses that challenge. He asked the Board to pass it as is without delay, so they can get working.
Commissioner Pritchett comment it is good to see Mr. Garvey again; she has a couple of requests for the Board; she does support tourism and the importance of Brevard County as a destination; she thinks the Board does need to look at the committed $12.4 million that is being done for the marketing; it says $15 but $2.67 million is already going towards lifeguards; this Board has an ability to look at these funds because they can be used for facilities, transportation, and certain other items, including the rest of the lifeguard funding; and Commissioner Feltner did a great job moving a lot of those funds over off of the weight on the General Fund to this. She mentioned there is still a delta this Board has to cover out of the General Fund; because the County is facing an uncertainty regarding what is coming up in the future with property tax revenues, not that it should ever be on the tourist development funds, but some of these funds can be used for tourist development and would relieve some of the pressure on the General Fund; there is $15 million in the advertising fund, $2.6 is going to lifeguards, which means there is $12.4 that is currently being used for advertising in this plan; and she asked if that is correct.
Mr. Cranis replied yes, however, $400,000 of that is being used for the grant program, so it is basically $12 million.
Commissioner Pritchett stated the amount that the County has to do is a 40 percent threshold so that delta that is left over of $758,000, she would like staff to identify what type of opportunities there would be for the County to use some of those monies on, which is the delta between the amount the County is allowed to use for different things; she does know that the capital fund has an availability as well; and she inquired if that is correct.
Mr. Cranis replied affirmatively, advising there is about $2.7 million unallocated funds in that.
Commissioner Pritchett stated she thinks it would important, not that this might not get approved, but to take it to the next meeting to give staff an opportunity to come back if there are any other opportunities; she would personally like to recommend that the County put all of the lifeguards on this time to alleviate some of the pressure that is going to be on the general fund; she is trying to find alternative revenue sources; and it is definitely not comfortable the Board had to do with the taxes this year. She noted she knows Commissioner Feltner did not support having to go over but it is something this Board had to do; she is looking for funds so here would be at least another pot that could be moved over to alleviate some of the pressure off the General Fund; she does not know where to put it right now, but there are a lot of air conditioners breaking in the County; this is general funds that there are still a lot of critical needs for; it would not be a bad idea to move it into the reserves until staff comes back with recommendations of where the funds need to go as well; she gave the Board Members a request from her; and what she is thinking is that if the Board just goes ahead and puts it off to the next meeting, so it has time to get some data from staff and review it to see if there is any other opportunities to move the funds with because ultimately it is on the Board because the Board is the elected body of how the funds move in the County.
Commissioner Feltner stated Item J.2. is sort of separate that the Chair wants to bring back in the future; and he asked if Commissioner Pritchett wants all of this Item to be tabled.
Chair Altman commented to be delayed.
Commissioner Pritchett stated just so the Board has time to look at it; she just started work on this Sunday night and she cannot talk to the other Board Members, so she had to come to the Board with it.
Commissioner Feltner stated he understands and there are couple of things that he thinks he could split with Commissioner Pritchett, if the Board passes J.2. today; first of all the Board could just pay for the rest of the lifeguards, 100 percent funded; he thinks that can be done, possibly some of that could come out of the capital and get moved to marketing and then pay for the lifeguards; by doing that, that is a General Fund obligation; if Commissioner Pritchett wants to free up General Fund dollars, that is the way to do it; it would free that up for staff; he would like to leave the rest of the money in capital because there is below $900,000; the Board had decided to build up capital again because in the last year it was below that amount; he would like to leave that for now, but he would do the lifeguards; item D where Commissioner Pritchett wants to change the Director, instead of at eh Director the County Manager will be able to access disaster funds, and he thinks that is fine; and he would go with Commissioner Pritchett on that.
Commissioner Pritchett commented she likes it; there is $2.5 million in the capital so she would like staff to come back if there is anything that was missed that they can identify, so this Board can vote where it wants to do that; that has to come from the County Commission; but she does believe the Board members need to have time to really take a little bit of time to study this so it does not do any knee-jerk reaction; but she likes the rest of it and she thinks it is a great marketing plan; these are just some options that she thought this Board should look at since it really is trying to find money and move money around right now, without hurting tourist development. She mentioned it might come back with just the lifeguards, but she would like for the Board members to have an opportunity to spend a little bit of time on it and look at it; if she could pick up the phone and call Commissioner Feltner she would have done it.
Commissioner Feltner asked if that is a motion.
Commissioner Pritchett stated she make a motion to table to the next regular meeting; and she inquired if that is going to hurt anything in doing that.
Mr. Cranis replied it would cause a delay in the fall campaign, but staff will work with it, whatever the Board wants to do.
Commissioner Pritchett asked about the budget meeting next week, and doing this as an add-on.
Commissioner Adkinson noted that would be fine.
Mr. Cranis stated that would be great; and he expressed his appreciation.
The Board denied tabling the Item to the Budget Hearing scheduled on September 22, 2026.

action_text:
Jim Liesenfelt, County Manager, stated this is what the Board asked staff to bring back at the last Board meeting; staff brought together an Agenda package that shows the different options for the fuel tax which is the one to five local option gas tax and as was mentioned the ninth cent gas tax; it was listed that it could be used for road repaving, resurfacing, drainage, covert replacement, drainage inspection, transit service, traffic operations, transportation construction, capital equipment, and some various other items; attached staff has put together a listing of how each of the counties implement their gas tax; there is a revenue generating option update from Public Works Department; and then there are some questions about electric vehicles, so staff provided some information on what different states do for the registration. He noted last but not least, there is a chart showing how much the gas tax has generated over the past five years; and staff stands ready to answer any questions the Board may have.
Mike Shah, Southeast Petroleum, stated he has lived and done business in Brevard County for more than 46 years; he cares deeply about the future of the community and the Space Coast; he is there to respectfully ask the Board to vote no on any additional local gas tax; he understands the County needs money for roads, drainage, and transportation; these are real needs and they should be addressed; but before adding another tax, one needs to ask what will be the economic consequences and have the propel of Brevard been given a proper voice. He mentioned Brevard County is different than many counties; everyday thousands of people travel into this County to work at the Kennedy Space Center, Cape Canaveral, Defense and Aerospace companies, construction projects, and other businesses; gasoline is a product where the price is displayed in huge numbers, right on the street, and consumers see every penny, just like right now at around $4.17 per gallon of unleaded gas and or $6 for diesel; if the County makes gasoline more expensive in Brevard County people who live or travel out of the County have a choice, some can fill up before entering or after leaving Brevard; when losing that gasoline customer, the business does not just lose gallons, the convenience store can lose the coffee, food, drinks, and other purchases that the customer would have made; and that affects local business independent operators and the employees. He commented if volume declines enough, businesses have to reduce expenses, reduce employee hours, or sometimes reduce their workforce; the County projects that this optional tax could generate approximately $9.1 million per year, but he would respectfully ask does that project fully consider changes in consumer behavior and the potential loss of fuel volume to surrounding counties; before approving this tax, please understand its complete economic impact, not only how much government expects to collect, but what it could cost local businesses and communities; also, most importantly, he believe the tax should have been placed before the voters of Brevard, but having the legal authority to impose a tax and deciding whether public should have a voice are two different questions; is additional transportation funding truly necessary, explain the need to people so they know where the exact money will go, show the project it will fund, and put it on the ballot and let the taxpayers decide; and Brevard County already has a six cent local option tax. He asked the Board to please not solve one problem by creating another problem for the residents, employees, and local businesses; he stated no additional gas tax without the voice of the people, let the voters decide; and he expressed his appreciation to the Board for listening and its service to Brevard County.
Richard Heffelfinger stated he it goes again; there is an opportunity to take some action that has already been offered so many times it is enough to gag a maggot; this was presented to the Board during budget workshops, the exact same numbers were given; now there is a little more information; at least there was some clarification about the electric vehicles because it is only a small percentage of the vehicles using this that would be not being hit; one can play that game about registration he does not care, but here is the thing, Brevard County has a lot of tourists that buy gas in Brevard County; he would rather the tourist pay a little extra and have the residents pay a little extra instead of the Board busting the cap to give $1.6 to road resurfacing; this thing is 8.2, wow that is some good money, the County could actually adjust; the $1.6 does not fix the road resurfacing, the County is billions of dollars in arrears on transportation, but every little bit helps; the County is already taxing the gas, why not just finish it off; there are some good numbers of revenue that comes on the gas taxes; he is seeing $23 million, $25 million, over the years; and this is just another nine and it is a good way to keep it off the backs of the County residents who are paying to make up the difference when there are options, and this is an option. He went on to say what he is saying is he wants the Board to pass tax the gas; he wants everybody in Brevard County to have to pay a little more for gas because he does not want to be paying for it out of his real estate tax; the Board talks about ways and being creative, finding ways to get revenue, and this is one; But the Board has to take the bite; it has been seen over and over again, but the Board refuses to do it; the County already has a whole load of them, and he asked what is one more; he asked the Board to take the bite and take the pressure off the real estate tax because if will not be able to rely on it if that amendment passes; the County is going to be hurting; and the Board better start ponying up. He noted it is going to take courage; he received a compliment from the Chairman about courage to come up and say the Board needs to take some action; there were a lot of things proposed; this was one of them; the Board can do it with a supermajority tonight; he asked them not to kick it down the road, it has been kicked down the road for years; the time to kick has stopped, do it now, get that money for 26/27; take some of the heat; it can re-spread the budgets and take some of that heat off the real estate tax; busting the cap does not look good; this is much easier than busting the cap; and the Board can blame him.
Chair Altman asked if the Board approves this, does it actually develop an ordinance and bring the ordinance back to the Commission for a vote; does the Board need to reach out to the cities; and does that require an interlocal agreement like the original gas tax required; and how that would be divided amongst the cities and the County.
Morris Richardson, County Attorney advised staff would work with the cities on the second local option five cent gas tax, like the first six cents, or there is a default formula that is provided with regard to the ninth cent; and he does not believe there is a municipal share for that, but Ms. Wall knows better than he; in order to levy it however, the County has to levy that by ordinance; there was no direction to have an ordinance today; an ordinance has not been advertised because staff did not have that Board direction; in order to do that to be effective January 1, 2027, it would have to be done by October 1; and the County has to advertise an ordinance for at least 10 days in advance; and the Board would be looking at a special meeting prior to the end of September, if a supermajority vote of the Board wanted to do that. He noted staff would prepare the ordinance and bring it back.
Chair Altman asked so to that point, to advertise an ordinance for consideration, not to pass the local option gas tax, but strictly to advertise the ordinance, does that require a super majority of is passage of the ordinance require super majority.
Attorney Richardson advised technically, a simple majority of the Board could direct him to prepare an ordinance and advertise it and call a special meeting; and as a practical matter, if the votes simply are not there, it may be an exercise in futility, but certainly three Board Members could make that direction and call for the advertisement, schedule the meeting, and all those things.
Chair Altman stated hypothetically staff advertises the ordinance; he wants to be clear, and he asked do they need to reach out to the cities for some sort of agreement or can the Board just pass the ordinance.
Attorney Richardson stated he thinks the ordinance would come first and staff would work with the cities on the agreement; or they could be working that simultaneously if there was clear direction that it was going to implement that.
Commissioner Goodson asked if anybody knows how this will affect construction, diesel, and stuff like that.
Chair Altman commented that is a good question and he asked if diesel is treated differently.
Mr. Liesenfelt state the way he understands it, the one through five would tax diesel; the County is already taxing diesel on the ninth cent; the ninth cent would only put an addition on gasoline.
Commissioner Goodson asked if it is true that even gasoline will affect construction; and does anybody know how much gasoline is bought for construction.
Mr. Liesenfelt responded by saying he does not have that information.
Commissioner Goodson stated he thinks that is something the Board would want to know before voting on this because if it votes on it, and it kills construction, he would find that strange, but maybe everybody else is happy with that.
Chair Altman stated one thing to keep in mind about construction is if the Board were to pass it, all that money would go toward construction, it would produce a significant amount of construction.
Commissioner Goodson commented he is not sure that is because if it goes toward construction and it is forcing people to buy gas to get out to Blue Origin or the Cape, it is going to kill that; and he asked if that is true.
Chair Altman stated he thinks the idea is to provide access to get to Blue Origin, the road is getting pretty crowded; that is probably a discussion and a debate the Board needs to have if it is considering this.
Commissioner Adkinson stated for her, she has talked before about the EV vehicles, but she is also not really very comfortable with the tax right now; everyone keeps saying it is getting difficult out there, so she is not necessarily for a gas tax now, but she is not opposed to placing it on the ballot to let the residents of Brevard County decide; and that is just her two cents.
Chair Altman thanked her for the input.
Commissioner Feltner stated the Board does not have to make the decision now to put something before the voters in 2028; and in fact, the Board can make a decision as late as July 2028 to put something before the voters.
Chair Altman stated that would be the first time this Board would be able to put it before the voters; and he inquired if that is correct, it has to be in a general election.
Attorney Richardson stated the referendum has to be on a general election ballot; the deadline for the November 2028 is going to be sometime in August 2028; and therefore, the Board has a lot of time between now and then, if it wants to go the referendum route, for staff to do an ordinance.
Commissioner Feltner stated the Board can come back after June break and start budget; as part of that it can decide to put this before the voters in 2028; and he is only saying that the Board does not need to take a vote today to put it before the voters in 2028.
Commissioner Pritchett stated she is out of here so she is not going to take any hit on this; she was willing if the Board wants to do it because at that time it is going to be near election time and everybody gets a little more hesitant; it is going to depend on whether anyone is willing to take the hit, which she hopes the Board members are because that is what makes public leadership fun, going ahead and doing what one knows is right…
Commissioner Feltner noted he was just making the distinction.
Commissioner Pritchett continued by saying if the Board is willing to do that, she is impressed.
Chair Altman asked if there needs to be a motion, he does not think there needs to be a motion on the floor.
Attorney Richardson advised this is just bringing back the request for discussion and direction; and he only needs a motion if the Board wishes to give any direction.
Chair Altman asked if there is any motion on this Item and if not he will move on.
The Board discussed but took no action on the consideration of a ninth-cent unleaded motor fuel tax and local option unleaded motor fuel gas tax.
